info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Provide an in-depth, citation-rich literature survey of tensegrity structure designs (both canonical and non-canonical) that have been described in the academic, patent, and grey literature. Include, at minimum:
(1) Canonical Snelson-class prismatic tensegrities (T-bar / T-prism / n-bar prisms, with the stable twist angle theta = pi/2 - pi/n), including T3 (3-bar), T4 (4-bar), T6, and stacked/columnar prisms; (2) Polyhedral / spherical tensegrities -- 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, the SUPERball-class geometry), expanded octahedron, truncated tetrahedron, truncated octahedron, dodecahedral / rhombic tensegrities, and higher-genus spherical tensegrities by Pugh, Burkhardt, Skelton, Connelly & Whiteley, and Tibert & Pellegrino; (3) Class-k tensegrities (k>=2) where k struts share a node, including Skelton's class-2 columns and class-3 plates, T-bar / D-bar / Y-bar units, and Bendsoe-Skelton optimal mass tensegrities; (4) Tensegrity beams, columns, plates, and cylindrical / cylindrical deployable tensegrity masts (Snelson 'Needle Tower', Pellegrino, Skelton & Nagase, Sultan & Skelton, Bel Hadj Ali, Smaili & Motro 'tensegrity ring'); (5) Tensegrity domes, cable-domes, and Geiger / Levy / Fuller geodesic-derived tensegrities, including the Seoul Olympic Gymnastics Hall and Georgia Dome cable-domes; (6) Bio-inspired and morphologically-novel tensegrities -- Levin's biotensegrity (spinal column, knee, shoulder, cytoskeleton), tensegrity robots (NASA SUPERball v1/v2, Berkeley ULTRA-Spine, Tensegrity Spine, T-bar quadrupeds, TenseBot, Spherobot, Mori & Hirose helical tensegrity, EVA series, snake/worm tensegrity robots), tensegrity wings/UAVs, tensegrity grippers, soft-tensegrity manipulators, MEMS / micro-tensegrities, origami- and kirigami-tensegrity hybrids, knitted / woven tensegrity textiles, and lattice/metamaterial tensegrities; (7) Tensegrity space structures and large deployable tensegrities (NASA TIPS, ESA tensegrity boom, Tibert/Pellegrino deployable masts, lunar/Mars habitats, Skelton's tensegrity wheel, ChemRover); (8) Modular and self-assembling tensegrities, including TetraSpine, ReBOT, and recent (2022-2026) work on adaptive, morphing, self-stressed, and energy-harvesting tensegrities; (9) Tensegrity-inspired metamaterials and architected unit cells used in additive manufacturing (3D-printed multi-material PETG/TPU and elastomer-rigid composites), including Fraternali, Rimoli, Pajunen, Pal et al. work on tensegrity lattices for impact absorption and wave control; (10) Non-Snelson topology generation methods (Tensegrity_gen, topology optimization, evolutionary search, machine-learning generative tensegrity design from 2020 onwards).

For each design family, give: design name + standard reference, node/strut/cable counts, characteristic geometric parameters and constraints, prestress / form-finding requirements, known self-equilibrated configurations, and at least one reference image with figure caption / source attribution (cite the original paper or open archive). Where possible include open-source / permissively-licensed sources (NASA NTRTsim, MOTES, Tensegrity_gen, Berkeley ULTRA-Spine, the Snelson archive, GrabCAD / Thingiverse) and indicate which designs have publicly available CAD / STL / URDF / mesh files.

Conclude with concrete recommendations for the BYU Mentored Research Grant project on multi-material 3D-printed tensegrity (PETG struts + TPU tendons, Bambu Lab H2D printer, target application: impact-absorbing crutch tip and architected energy-absorbing lattices): which 5-10 tensegrity designs would be most promising as starting geometries for parametric / Bayesian-optimization design exploration, with rationale and the specific geometric/material parameters that should be exposed as design variables.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Tensegrity structures are prestressed and self-stable pin-connected frameworks built up mainly from two kind of elements, in compression (bars) and in tension (tendons). It has been 75 years since the first official appearance of tensegrity, although the present paper includes proof that states that they are in fact more than 100 years old. Throughout these years, tensegrity structures have been capturing engineers’, architects’ and artists’ attention with their peculiar properties. In the last decade, new applications have been found based on tensegrity, although there are not any compilations about them. This paper aims to fill this gap by giving an overview of all the recent real applications that tensegrity has had during its short life, at the same time exposing its potential in all the fields it has contributed to (AEC, robotics, space, etc.) The methodology for performing this review has been revisiting the most relevant publications in several scientific databases. This has led to a new discovery: the first cable-dome by Snelson. As a conclusion, tensegrity has been providing useful solutions to previous problems since they have appeared, but their potential can still grow in an exponential way due to the new technologies and discoveries of the last decade.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We try to make a long way short by proceeding per exempla from Kenneth Snelson’s sculptures and Richard Buckminster Fuller’s coinage of the term tensegrity to modern tensegrity metamaterials. We document the passage from initial interest in tensegrity frameworks for their visual impact to today’s interest, driven by their peculiar structural performances. In the past seventy years, the early art pieces and roofing structural complexes have been followed by formalization of the principles governing the form-finding property of ‘pure’ tensegrity structures and by engineering hybridization leading to a host of diverse practical applications, such as variable-geometry civil engineering structures, on-earth and in-orbit deployable structures and robots, and finally to recent and promising studies on tensegrity metamaterials and small-scale tensegrity structures.

Abstract:
Tensegrity robots are a class of compliant robots that have many desirable traits when designing mass efficient systems that must interact with uncertain environments. Various promising control approaches have been proposed for tensegrity systems in simulation. Unfortunately, state estimation methods for tensegrity robots have not yet been thoroughly studied. In this paper, we present the design and evaluation of a state estimator for tensegrity robots. This state estimator will enable existing and future control algorithms to transfer from simulation to hardware. Our approach is based on the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and combines inertial measurements, ultra wideband time-of-flight ranging measurements, and actuator state information. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on the SUPERball, a tensegrity based planetary exploration robotic prototype. In particular, we conduct tests for evaluating both the robot's success in estimating global position in relation to fixed ranging base stations during rolling maneuvers as well as local behavior due to small-amplitude deformations induced by cable actuation.

Abstract:
Tensegrity robots, composed of rigid rods connected by elastic cables, have a number of unique properties that make them appealing for use as planetary exploration rovers. However, control of tensegrity robots remains a difficult problem due to their unusual structures and complex dynamics. In this work, we show how locomotion gaits can be learned automatically using a novel extension of mirror descent guided policy search (MDGPS) applied to periodic locomotion movements, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on tensegrity robot locomotion. We evaluate our method with real-world and simulated experiments on the SUPERball tensegrity robot, showing that the learned policies generalize to changes in system parameters, unreliable sensor measurements, and variation in environmental conditions, including varied terrains and a range of different gravities. Our experiments demonstrate that our method not only learns fast, power-efficient feedback policies for rolling gaits, but that these policies can succeed with only the limited onboard sensing provided by SUPERball's accelerometers. We compare the learned feedback policies to learned open-loop policies and hand-engineered controllers, and demonstrate that the learned policy enables the first continuous, reliable locomotion gait for the real SUPERball robot. Our code and supplementary material is available from http://rll.berkeley.edu/drl_tensegrity.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A bistable response is an innate feature of tensegrity metamaterials, which is a conundrum to attain in other metamaterials, since it ushers unconventional static and dynamical mechanical behaviors. This paper investigates the design, modeling, fabrication and testing of bistable lattices with tensegrity architecture and nanoscale features. First, a method to design bistable lattices tessellating tensegrity units is formulated. The additive manufacturing of these structures is performed through multiphoton lithography, which enables the fabrication of microscale structures with nanoscale features and extremely high resolution. Different modular lattices, comprised of struts with 250 nm minimum radius, are tested under loading-unloading uniaxial compression nanoindentation tests. The compression tests confirmed the activation of the designed bistable twisting mechanism in the examined lattices, combined with a moderate viscoelastic response. The force-displacement plots of the 3D assemblies of bistable tensegrity prisms reveal a softening behavior during the loading from the primary stable configuration and a subsequent snapping event that drives the structure into a secondary stable configuration. The twisting mechanism that characterizes such a transition is preserved after unloading and during repeated loading-unloading cycles. The results of the present study elucidate that fabrication of multistable tensegrity lattices is highly feasible via multiphoton lithography and promulgates the fabrication of multi-cell tensegrity metamaterials with unprecedented static and dynamic responses.</jats:p>

    issue = "1",
    issn = "1063-6536"
}


Abstract:
Robots with flexible spines based on tensegrity structures have potential advantages over traditional designs with rigid torsos. However, these robots can be difficult to control due to their high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics and actuator constraints. This article presents two controllers for tensegrity spine robots, using model-predictive control (MPC) and inverse statics (IS) optimization. The controllers introduce two different approaches to making the control problem computationally tractable. The first utilizes smoothing terms in the MPC problem. The second uses a new IS optimization algorithm, which gives the first feasible solutions to the problem for certain tensegrity robots, to generate reference input trajectories in combination with MPC. Tracking the IS reference input trajectory significantly reduces the number of tuning parameters. The controllers are validated against simulations of 2-D and 3-D tensegrity spines. Both approaches show noise insensitivity and low tracking error and can be used for different control goals. The results here demonstrate the first closed-loop control of such structures.

Abstract:
Soft spherical tensegrity robots are novel steerable mobile robotic platforms that are compliant, lightweight, and robust. The geometry of these robots is suitable for rolling locomotion, and they achieve this motion by properly deforming their structures using carefully chosen actuation strategies. The objective of this work is to consolidate and add to our research to date on methods for realizing rolling locomotion of spherical tensegrity robots. To predict the deformation of tensegrity structures when their member forces are varied, we introduce a modified version of the dynamic relaxation technique and apply it to our tensegrity robots. In addition, we present two techniques to find desirable deformations and actuation strategies that would result in robust rolling locomotion of the robots. The first one relies on the greedy search that can quickly find solutions, and the second one uses a multigeneration Monte Carlo method that can find suboptimal solutions with a higher quality. The methods are illustrated and validated both in simulation and with our hardware robots, which show that our methods are viable means of realizing robust and steerable rolling locomotion of spherical tensegrity robots.

Abstract:
The properties of materials and structures typically remain fixed after being designed and manufactured. There is a growing interest in systems with the capability of altering their behaviors without changing geometries or material constitutions, because such reprogrammable behaviors could unlock multiple functionalities within a single design. We introduce an optimization-driven approach, based on multi-objective magneto-mechanical topology optimization, to design magneto-active metamaterials and structures whose properties can be seamlessly reprogrammed by switching on and off the external stimuli fields. This optimized material system exhibits one response under pure mechanical loading, and switches to a distinct response under joint mechanical and magnetic stimuli. We discover and experimentally demonstrate magneto-mechanical metamaterials and metastructures that realize a wide range of reprogrammable responses, including multi-functional actuation responses, adaptable snap-buckling behaviors, switchable deformation modes, and tunable bistability. The proposed approach paves the way for promising applications such as magnetic actuators, soft robots, and energy harvesters.

Abstract:
Natural materials typically exhibit irregular and non-periodic architectures, endowing them with compelling functionalities such as body protection, camouflage, and mechanical stress modulation. Among these functionalities, mechanical stress modulation is crucial for homeostasis regulation and tissue remodeling. Here, we uncover the relationship between stress modulation functionality and the irregularity of bio-inspired architected materials by a generative computational framework. This framework optimizes the spatial distribution of a limited set of basic building blocks and uses these blocks to assemble irregular materials with heterogeneous, disordered microstructures. Despite being irregular and non-periodic, the assembled materials display spatially varying properties that precisely modulate stress distribution towards target values in various control regions and load cases, echoing the robust stress modulation capability of natural materials. The performance of the generated irregular architected materials is experimentally validated with 3D printed physical samples — a good agreement with target stress distribution is observed. Owing to its capability to redirect loads while keeping a proper amount of stress to stimulate bone repair, we demonstrate the potential application of the stress-programmable architected materials as support in orthopedic femur restoration.

Abstract:

 This study presents the customization of bicycle stems to their cyclists’ specificities by using a factorial plan and generative design approach. Five non-professional cyclists participated in the study. The tests were performed on a home-made static bicycle bench which has instrumented pedals and strain gauges on the handlebars and the saddle. A design of experiment with three parameters on two levels is employed to identify the cyclists with the greatest influence from the bicycle settings. The three parameters are pedaling rate, stem length and saddle height. The responses studied are divided into two categories. The first is focused on the behavior of the structure, via strain gauges and instrumented pedals. The forces applied by the participants on the handlebars, the saddle as well as the pedaling power are investigated. The second category focuses on movements through video recordings. The mean angular amplitude of the knee and hip is studied. It was found that three participants out of five were more sensitive to the modifications of the handlebars’ position and the saddle height. The generative design of the bicycle stem was conducted using the specificities of these three riders as load cases. The optimized stems were validated using finite element analysis. They are very organic, which is way different from the commercially available stems. They are also different from one another, proving that it may be worth looking into this tool to push bike optimization to its maximum, for people sensitives to the geometric settings of their bicycle.

Abstract:
Analytical paradigms have limited conventional form-finding methods of tensegrities; therefore, an innovative approach is urgently needed. This paper proposes a new form-finding method based on state-of-the-art deep learning techniques. One of the statical paradigms, a force density method, is substituted for trained deep neural networks to obtain necessary information of tensegrities. It is based on the differential evolution algorithm, where the eigenvalue decomposition process of the force density matrix and the process of the equilibrium matrix are not needed to find the feasible sets of nodal coordinates. Three well-known tensegrity examples including a 2D two-strut, a 3D-truncated tetrahedron and an icosahedron tensegrity are presented for numerical verifications. The cases of the ReLU and Leaky ReLU activation functions show better results than those of the ELU and SELU. Moreover, the results of the proposed method are in good agreement with the analytical super-stable lines. Three examples show that the proposed method exhibits more uniform final shapes of tensegrity, and much faster convergence history than those of the conventional one.

Abstract:
In this paper, a new form-finding analysis methodology for a class 2 tensegrity robot is proposed. The methodology consists of two steps: first, the analysis of the possible geometric configurations of the robot is carried out through the results of the kinematic position analysis; and, second, from the static analysis, the equilibrium positions of the robot are found, which represents its workspace. Both kinematics and static analysis are resolved in a closed-form using basic tools of linear algebra instead of the strategies used in literature. Four numerical experiments are presented using the finite element analysis software ANSYS©. Additionally, a comparison between the results of the form-finding analysis methodology proposed and the ANSYS© results is presented.

Abstract:
Form-finding processes are an integral part of structural design. Because of their limitations, the classic approaches to finding a form – such as hanging models and the soap-film analogy – play only a minor role. The various possibilities of digital experimentation in the context of structural optimisation create new options for the designer generating forms, while enabling control over a wide variety of parameters. A complete mapping of the mechanical properties of a structure in a continuum mechanics model is possible but so are simplified modelling strategies which take into account only the most important properties of the structure, such as iteratively approximating to a solution via representations of kinematic states. Form finding is thus an extremely complex process, determined both by the freely selected parameters and by design decisions.

Abstract:
This paper presents a study on form-finding of four-stage class one self-equilibrated spine biotensegrity models. Advantageous features such as slenderness and natural curvature of the human spine, as well as the stabilizing network that consists of the spinal column and muscles, were modeled and incorporated in the mathematical formulation of the spine biotensegrity models. Form-finding analysis, which involved determination of independent self-equilibrium stress modes using generalized inverse and their linear combination, was carried out. Form-finding strategy for searching the self-equilibrated models was studied through two approaches: application of various combinations of (1) twist angles and (2) nodal coordinates. A total of three configurations of the spine biotensegrity models with different sizes of triangular cell were successfully established for the first time in this study. All members in the spine biotensegrity models satisfied the assumption of linear elastic material behavior. With the established spine biotensegrity model, the advantageous characteristics of flexibility and versatility of movement can be further studied for potential application in deployable structures and flexible arm in the robotic industry.

Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials Valid Text Names: 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 1-2', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 2-4', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 4-5', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 5-8', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 8-9', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 9-10', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 10-10' BibTex: @article{ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity, author = "Ruffini, Franco N. and Rimoli, Julian J.", title = "Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials", year = "2026", journal = "npj Metamaterials", volume = "2", month = "Mar", doi = "10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1" } Abstract: Abstract

Failure in most material systems is characterized by strain localization, where deformation concentrates within a narrow region. Recently, a class of truss-based metamaterials has been shown to undergo severe deformation without exhibiting localization [1]. The mechanisms underlying this unusual delocalized response remain unknown. Here, we employ graph theory to elucidate the origins of this behavior. Each lattice is represented as a pair of graphs—the tension and compression networks—and their topological properties are quantified using graph-theoretic metrics. We find that the onset of localization correlates strongly with connectivity measures of these graphs. Specifically, deformation delocalization arises from an asymmetry in connectivity between these networks: when the tension graph remains more connected than the compression graph, deformation spreads throughout the structure instead of localizing. Connectivity measures such as average global efficiency[2] capture this transition quantitatively. This framework provides design principles for creating materials and metamaterials that intrinsically resist failure localization.

The excerpt defines tensegrity as a self-equilibrium system of continuous prestressed cables and discrete compression bars, and contrasts true tensegrity systems with cable-dome variants. Geiger adapted Fuller’s idea to create a 'cable dome' that was applied to the circular roof structures for the Seoul Olympic Games (Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas, 1986), but the paper notes these cable domes "could not be considered as an actual Tensegrity system, because the compressed ring is not inside the set of cables." Levy later revised the layout and built the Georgia Dome (1992) in a quasi-elliptical shape. The author also cites work on double-layer grid tensegrity systems. The paper describes numerical analysis of tensegrity structures as geometrically non-linear, requiring an iterative determination of the initial geometrical equilibrium and a two-phase analysis (initial equilibrium then static analysis), with the Newton–Raphson method used for incremental non-linear solution. The excerpt does not discuss deployable masts or works by Snelson, Tibert or Pellegrino.

| Canonical prism | 4-bar prism (T4, 4-strut simplex) | 4 | 12 | 8 | Regular prism-like simplex; one base rotated 135° relative to the other in Sabouni-Zawadzka’s 4-strut simplex lattice cell; often treated as extreme/quasi-bimode metamaterial unit cell | 1 | Self-stress plus member stiffness tune soft/stiff modes; continuum-homogenization for lattice behavior (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000035) | Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2019; Sabouni-Zawadzka 2020 (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000035) |

| Polyhedral / spherical | Tensegrity icosahedron (6-strut) | 6 | 24 outer; +12 inner in payload variant | not stated in retrieved context | Jessen/orthogonal-icosahedron / SUPERball-class spherical 6-bar topology; rolling-friendly spherical envelope | 1 | Prestressed outer spring-cable network; dynamic simulation in Euler–Lagrange and NTRT/Bullet frameworks (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009) | SunSpiral et al. 2015; Sabelhaus et al. 2015 (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009) |

{"answer": "# Comprehensive Literature Survey of Tensegrity Structure Designs

## 1. Introduction

Tensegrity ("tensional integrity") structures comprise isolated compression members (struts/bars) suspended within a continuous network of tension members (cables/tendons), achieving self-equilibrium through internal prestress. Since Kenneth Snelson's 1948 X-piece sculpture and R. Buckminster Fuller's coinage of the term, tensegrity has evolved from art into a rich engineering paradigm spanning architecture, robotics, metamaterials, biology, and space exploration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000018). This survey systematically catalogs the major tensegrity design families described in the academic, patent, and grey literature, and concludes with specific recommendations for a BYU multi-material 3D-printing project.

The following master table organizes the principal tensegrity design families, their geometric characteristics, and key references:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 2. Canonical Snelson-Class Prismatic Tensegrities

### 2.1 Three-Bar Prism (T3 / Simplex)
The simplest true tensegrity is the 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3): 3 struts, 9 cables (minimal) or 12 cables (non-minimal), and 6 nodes. Two triangular end-polygons are connected by struts with a characteristic stable twist angle θ = π/2 − π/n; for n = 3, θ = 30° (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). The T3 possesses one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent self-stress state; the mechanism is a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases, stabilized by the self-stress (pqac-00000036). Oliveira and Skelton present this as the foundational "regular minimal tensegrity prism," noting that non-minimal variants with 12 strings provide higher stiffness and eliminate soft modes (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Four-Bar Prism (T4 / 4-Strut Simplex)
The 4-strut simplex consists of 4 struts and 12 cables arranged in an 8-node prism with one base rotated 135° relative to the other. Sabouni-Zawadzka and Gilewski classify it as a "quasi-bimode" extreme metamaterial unit cell, featuring stiff, soft, and medium extensional modes plus high and low shear modes. The self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio serve as primary tuning parameters (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040).

### 2.3 Higher-Order Prisms and Stacked Columns
The n-bar prism family generalizes to T6 (θ = 60°) and beyond. Prism twist angles cluster near 30–36° with cable pretension in the 1.8–2.5% engineering strain range for typical designs (pqac-00000000). Snelson's iconic Needle Tower I (1968) and Needle Tower II (1969) are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms to form columnar masts (pqac-00000018). Yildiz and Lesieutre developed effective continuum beam stiffness properties for n-strut cylindrical tensegrity towers, enabling homogenized analysis of long stacked-prism columns for space applications.

---

## 3. Polyhedral / Spherical Tensegrities

### 3.1 Six-Strut Tensegrity Icosahedron
The 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (also called Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron) is the canonical spherical tensegrity: 6 struts and 24 cables. This topology forms the basis of the NASA SUPERball robot, where the 2015 prototype featured 1.7 m struts, ~21 kg mass, 24 spring-cable assemblies, and 12 BLDC actuators (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). A payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies for payload suspension (pqac-00000007).

### 3.2 Expanded Octahedron
The expanded octahedron tensegrity has been studied as a metamaterial unit cell exhibiting three stiff modes, one purely soft mode, and two quasi-soft modes, with the largest positive-definite elasticity region among five compared regular tensegrity modules (pqac-00000035). Vangelatos et al. fabricated expanded-octahedron-based bistable lattices using multiphoton lithography at nanoscale (minimum strut radii ~250 nm), demonstrating preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000041).

### 3.3 Truncated Tetrahedron
The truncated tetrahedron module is identified as the most "extreme" regular tensegrity unit cell, featuring three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes (classified as a "trimode" material). However, its required self-stress and stiffness ranges lie beyond current practical fabrication limits (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038).

### 3.4 Truncated Octahedron (Rimoli Cell)
The truncated octahedron tensegrity cell, introduced by Rimoli and Pal, has 12 struts and 36 cables and is inherently space-tileable. This cell is the foundation of the most important recent work on tensegrity metamaterials. Bauer et al. demonstrated that recursive reflection of truncated-octahedron cells into 2×2×2 and larger supercells creates metamaterials with isolated compression-member loops, suppressing localized failure and achieving up to 25-fold enhancement in deformability and orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption relative to same-strength conventional lattice architectures (pqac-00000028). Pajunen et al. developed a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity with post-buckling stability and load-limiting behavior, validated through both quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact experiments (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030).

---

## 4. Class-k Tensegrities

Skelton defines a "class-k" tensegrity as one in which at most k rigid bodies share a node. Class-1 tensegrities have no strut-to-strut connections (the canonical definition), while higher classes permit shared nodes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

### 4.1 T-Bar and D-Bar Units
The **T-bar** unit replaces a single compression bar of length ℓ₀ with an internally tensegritized subassembly: in the cited example, 4 bars and 16 strings forming a class-4 tensegrity. Mass reduction occurs when the internal angle α₁ < 45° (pqac-00000031). The **D-bar** is the dual of the T-bar, obtained by exchanging bars and strings; it is a class-2 tensegrity with string-to-string connections (pqac-00000031). These building blocks enable Skelton's minimum-mass optimization framework.

### 4.2 Minimum-Mass Columns and Plates
Skelton and de Oliveira derive closed-form optimal mass expressions for class-2 tensegrity cylinders parameterized by radius R, half-bay height z, helix angle φ, and complexity q. The normalized mass J = Js + Jb is minimized under material yield constraints, with optimal complexity q* balancing structural efficiency against joint mass penalties (pqac-00000032). For any given aspect ratio ρ and complexity q, the optimal bending angle satisfies tan β* = ρ^(1/q), with asymptotic minimal cost J*∞ = 2 ln ρ⁻¹ as q → ∞ (pqac-00000031).

---

## 5. Tensegrity Domes and Cable-Domes

### 5.1 Geiger Cable-Dome (Seoul Olympic Halls)
David Geiger adapted Fuller's Aspension Dome concept into radial cable-and-strut domes for the Seoul Olympic Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas (1986/1988). These are technically "cable-domes" rather than pure tensegrities because the outer compression ring is not embedded within the cable network (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018). Micheletti and Podio-Guidugli trace the lineage from Fuller's bicycle-wheel-like arrangement through Geiger's implementation (pqac-00000018).

### 5.2 Levy Cable-Dome (Georgia Dome)
Levy revised Geiger's radial layout with a triangulated cable network for the Georgia Dome (1992). Fu's nonlinear FE analysis showed that the primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section, with recommendations to increase prestress in inner cables for enhanced capacity (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). The Georgia Dome used φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires (1670 N/mm²) and Q345 circular tube struts (345 N/mm²) under 0.6 kN/m² uniform roof load (pqac-00000015).

---

## 6. Bio-Inspired and Morphologically Novel Tensegrities

### 6.1 Biotensegrity (Levin, Ingber)
Levin's biotensegrity framework models musculoskeletal structures—spine, shoulder, pelvis—as "continuous tension, discontinuous compression" systems where bones act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Ingber's cellular tensegrity model demonstrates that cells use tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: actin-myosin filaments generate contractile tension (prestress), microtubules serve as compression struts, and intermediate filaments act as guy wires (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). This hierarchical principle operates across scales from single proteins to whole organisms, with mechanotransduction enabled by long-range force transmission through the tensegrity network (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026).

### 6.2 Tensegrity Robots
**NASA SUPERball v1/v2**: A 6-strut icosahedron robot for planetary exploration, featuring 24 spring-cable assemblies and 12 actuators. The v1 (2015) measured ~1.7 m diameter, ~21 kg, with passive cable stiffness ~998 N/m and nominal actuated tension ~250 N (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). SUPERball v2 was redesigned to survive impact velocities upward of 8 m/s with 24 actuators and compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch). The **NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT)** is an open-source simulator built on the Bullet Physics engine, released for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

**Berkeley ULTRA-Spine**: A flexible actuated spine robot using stacked tensegrity vertebra modules, controlled via model-predictive control with inverse statics optimization (pqac-00000007). The TT-3 robot from UC Berkeley is a modular, rod-centered 6-bar tensegrity with distributed actuation and control architecture.

---

## 7. Tensegrity Space Structures and Deployable Systems

### 7.1 Deployable Tensegrity Masts
Tibert and Pellegrino developed deployable tensegrity mast concepts using stacked Snelson-type prisms, investigating both strut-mode deployment for eight-stage masts and tendon-controlled strategies (pqac-00000033). Sultan and Skelton proposed cable-controlled deployment following equilibrium manifolds to maintain structural integrity throughout transformation (pqac-00000034).

### 7.2 Deployable Antenna Patents
**US 6,441,801 B1** (Knight et al., 2002): A screw-motion-driven tensegrity antenna with a parallel-platform architecture consisting of upper hexagonal platform and lower hexagonal base connected by compression strut and tension tie leg pairs (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). **US 6,542,132 B2** (Stern, 2003): A deployable reflector antenna with tensegrity support architecture and mounting frame for improved specific mass and compact stowage (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).

### 7.3 Wave Generation Patent
**US 8,616,328 B2** (Daraio, 2013): A tensegrity apparatus composed of multiple tensegrity units for transmitting solitary waves with adjustable profiles into materials or structures, enabling nondestructive evaluation applications (pqac-00000049).

---

## 8. Tensegrity-Inspired Metamaterials and Additive Manufacturing

### 8.1 Truncated Octahedron Lattices (Rimoli, Pajunen, Bauer)
The truncated-octahedron tensegrity cell (12 struts, 36 cables) is the leading architecture for 3D-printable impact-absorbing metamaterials. Pajunen et al. developed a single-material 3D-printable equivalent validated through ABAQUS simulations, quasi-static compression, and drop-weight impact tests (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030). Bauer et al. achieved unprecedented failure resistance with up to 25-fold deformability enhancement and orders-of-magnitude increased energy absorption through delocalized deformation enabled by compression-member discontinuity (pqac-00000028). Ruffini and Rimoli used graph theory to show that deformation delocalization correlates with asymmetric tension-compression connectivity, providing design principles for failure-resistant metamaterials.

### 8.2 Tunable Tensegrity Tessellations
Liu et al. developed a cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation block (13 struts, 96 cables) with 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms, using polymer-like material properties (E_S = 2600 MPa, E_C = 12 MPa) representative of multi-material 3D printing. Computational homogenization demonstrated rich tunability of effective stiffness and bandgaps (pqac-00000006).

### 8.3 Bistable Tensegrity Units
Intrigila et al. fabricated bistable double-triangular-prism units via stereolithography, demonstrating snap-through behavior with preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000005). Vangelatos et al. extended this to nanoscale using multiphoton lithography with 250 nm minimum feature sizes (pqac-00000041).

### 8.4 Simplex-Based Lattice Metamaterials
Sabouni-Zawadzka systematically compared five regular tensegrity unit cells—4-strut simplex (quasi-bimode), 3-strut simplex (quasi-trimode), expanded octahedron (quasi-trimode), truncated tetrahedron (trimode), and X-module (unimode)—identifying soft and stiff deformation modes via eigenanalysis of equivalent elasticity matrices (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038). Self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio are the primary tuning parameters, with six representative deformation modes: stiff, soft, and medium extensional, plus high (double) and low shear (pqac-00000040).

---

## 9. Topology Generation and Computational Design Methods

### 9.1 Form-Finding Methods
Tibert and Pellegrino's 2003 review established the standard taxonomy of form-finding approaches: force-density methods, energy minimization, dynamic relaxation, and analytical solutions for regular topologies (pqac-00000017). Recent advances include genetic-algorithm-based total potential energy minimization for free-form tensegrities (Uzun 2017) and deep neural networks for form-finding that substitute trained DNNs for eigenvalue decomposition of force-density matrices (Lee et al. 2022). Graph neural networks have also been applied to tensegrity form-finding (Shao et al. 2024).

### 9.2 Open-Source Software
Key open-source tools include: **NTRT (NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit)**, built on the Bullet Physics engine for tensegrity robot simulation (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012); **MOTES (MOdeling TENsegrity Structures)**, a MATLAB-based open-source tool by Skelton's group for statics, dynamics, and form-finding of general tensegrity systems; and various research codes for computational homogenization of tensegrity metamaterials.

### 9.3 Elastic Lattice Patent for Tensegrity Robots
**US 2019/0382995 A1** (Chen, 2019): An elastic lattice platform for rapid prototyping of tensegrity structures and robots, where tensile members form a spatially defined structure without compressive members touching.

---

## 10. Recommendations for BYU Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity Project

For the BYU Mentored Research Grant project targeting impact-absorbing crutch tips and energy-absorbing lattices using PETG struts + TPU tendons on a Bambu Lab H2D printer, the following table ranks the most promising starting geometries:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key Rationale and Parameter Recommendations

**Top Priority: Truncated Octahedron Cell (Rank 1).** This cell has the strongest experimental validation for impact absorption (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Its 12-strut/36-cable topology maps naturally to PETG compression members and TPU tension members. The Bambu H2D's multi-material capability can print PETG struts with TPU tendons in a single build, potentially eliminating post-assembly. Critical design variables for Bayesian optimization include: unit-cell edge length (5–20 mm), strut diameter (0.8–3 mm), TPU tendon diameter (0.4–1.5 mm), initial tendon prestrain (0–10%), node fillet radius, and lattice relative density (5–30%).

**Calibration Benchmark: T3 Simplex (Rank 2).** The 3-bar prism (3 struts, 9 cables, 6 nodes) is the ideal calibration geometry because it has a single self-stress state and single mechanism, enabling clean validation of PETG/TPU constitutive models and the prestress-printing workflow before scaling to more complex cells (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036).

**Stacked Prismatic Column (Rank 7).** Particularly suited to the crutch-tip application because its axial geometry matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios. Progressive bay collapse/twisting under axial impact can absorb energy through multiple stages, and functionally graded stiffness along the column height can be achieved by varying bay parameters.

**Material-Specific Parameters for Bayesian Optimization:**
- **PETG struts**: diameter (0.8–4 mm), wall thickness if hollow (0.4–1.2 mm), length/slenderness ratio (critical for Euler buckling plateau)
- **TPU tendons**: durometer (80A–95A), cross-section (0.4–2 mm diameter), initial stretch/prestrain (0–15%)
- **Interface**: node geometry/fillet radius, PETG-TPU bonding area, overhang angle constraints
- **Lattice-level**: cell count per axis (2×2×2 to 6×6×6), grading function, boundary/skin conditions, overall relative density

**Open-Source Resources:** The NASA NTRT simulator (open-source, GitHub) provides validated physics for tensegrity dynamics. MOTES (MATLAB open-source by Skelton's group) handles statics and form-finding. For CAD generation, the parametric geometry of all recommended cells can be scripted in Python/OpenSCAD from published node coordinates. The Pajunen/Rimoli truncated-octahedron cell geometry is fully specified in the literature and reproducible for STL generation (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

---

## 11. Conclusion

This survey documents the remarkable breadth of tensegrity structural designs spanning seven decades—from Snelson's original prismatic sculptures through NASA's SUPERball planetary lander to Rimoli's failure-resistant metamaterials. For the BYU multi-material 3D-printing project, the truncated-octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell emerges as the highest-priority starting geometry due to its validated impact performance, space-tileability, and natural compatibility with PETG-strut/TPU-tendon multi-material fabrication (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). The 3-bar simplex provides the ideal calibration benchmark (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036), while the 4-strut simplex and expanded octahedron offer rich intermediate complexity for parametric exploration (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). Bistable double-prism units add snap-through energy absorption capabilities particularly suited to crutch-tip applications (pqac-00000036). The stacked prismatic column geometry most naturally matches the axial loading profile of a crutch tip (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018). All recommended geometries have sufficient published geometric specifications for parametric CAD generation, and the rich design variable space—spanning strut/tendon dimensions, prestrain, cell count, grading, and material selection—is well-suited to Bayesian optimization for systematic performance improvement."}
