{"answer": "# Comprehensive Literature Survey of Tensegrity Structure Designs

## 1. Introduction

Tensegrity ("tensional integrity") structures comprise isolated compression members (struts/bars) suspended within a continuous network of tension members (cables/tendons), achieving self-equilibrium through internal prestress. Since Kenneth Snelson's 1948 X-piece sculpture and R. Buckminster Fuller's coinage of the term, tensegrity has evolved from art into a rich engineering paradigm spanning architecture, robotics, metamaterials, biology, and space exploration (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000018). This survey systematically catalogs the major tensegrity design families described in the academic, patent, and grey literature, and concludes with specific recommendations for a BYU multi-material 3D-printing project.

The following master table organizes the principal tensegrity design families, their geometric characteristics, and key references:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 2. Canonical Snelson-Class Prismatic Tensegrities

### 2.1 Three-Bar Prism (T3 / Simplex)
The simplest true tensegrity is the 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3): 3 struts, 9 cables (minimal) or 12 cables (non-minimal), and 6 nodes. Two triangular end-polygons are connected by struts with a characteristic stable twist angle θ = π/2 − π/n; for n = 3, θ = 30° (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). The T3 possesses one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent self-stress state; the mechanism is a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases, stabilized by the self-stress (pqac-00000036). Oliveira and Skelton present this as the foundational "regular minimal tensegrity prism," noting that non-minimal variants with 12 strings provide higher stiffness and eliminate soft modes (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Four-Bar Prism (T4 / 4-Strut Simplex)
The 4-strut simplex consists of 4 struts and 12 cables arranged in an 8-node prism with one base rotated 135° relative to the other. Sabouni-Zawadzka and Gilewski classify it as a "quasi-bimode" extreme metamaterial unit cell, featuring stiff, soft, and medium extensional modes plus high and low shear modes. The self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio serve as primary tuning parameters (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040).

### 2.3 Higher-Order Prisms and Stacked Columns
The n-bar prism family generalizes to T6 (θ = 60°) and beyond. Prism twist angles cluster near 30–36° with cable pretension in the 1.8–2.5% engineering strain range for typical designs (pqac-00000000). Snelson's iconic Needle Tower I (1968) and Needle Tower II (1969) are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms to form columnar masts (pqac-00000018). Yildiz and Lesieutre developed effective continuum beam stiffness properties for n-strut cylindrical tensegrity towers, enabling homogenized analysis of long stacked-prism columns for space applications.

---

## 3. Polyhedral / Spherical Tensegrities

### 3.1 Six-Strut Tensegrity Icosahedron
The 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (also called Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron) is the canonical spherical tensegrity: 6 struts and 24 cables. This topology forms the basis of the NASA SUPERball robot, where the 2015 prototype featured 1.7 m struts, ~21 kg mass, 24 spring-cable assemblies, and 12 BLDC actuators (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). A payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies for payload suspension (pqac-00000007).

### 3.2 Expanded Octahedron
The expanded octahedron tensegrity has been studied as a metamaterial unit cell exhibiting three stiff modes, one purely soft mode, and two quasi-soft modes, with the largest positive-definite elasticity region among five compared regular tensegrity modules (pqac-00000035). Vangelatos et al. fabricated expanded-octahedron-based bistable lattices using multiphoton lithography at nanoscale (minimum strut radii ~250 nm), demonstrating preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000041).

### 3.3 Truncated Tetrahedron
The truncated tetrahedron module is identified as the most "extreme" regular tensegrity unit cell, featuring three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes (classified as a "trimode" material). However, its required self-stress and stiffness ranges lie beyond current practical fabrication limits (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038).

### 3.4 Truncated Octahedron (Rimoli Cell)
The truncated octahedron tensegrity cell, introduced by Rimoli and Pal, has 12 struts and 36 cables and is inherently space-tileable. This cell is the foundation of the most important recent work on tensegrity metamaterials. Bauer et al. demonstrated that recursive reflection of truncated-octahedron cells into 2×2×2 and larger supercells creates metamaterials with isolated compression-member loops, suppressing localized failure and achieving up to 25-fold enhancement in deformability and orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption relative to same-strength conventional lattice architectures (pqac-00000028). Pajunen et al. developed a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity with post-buckling stability and load-limiting behavior, validated through both quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact experiments (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030).

---

## 4. Class-k Tensegrities

Skelton defines a "class-k" tensegrity as one in which at most k rigid bodies share a node. Class-1 tensegrities have no strut-to-strut connections (the canonical definition), while higher classes permit shared nodes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

### 4.1 T-Bar and D-Bar Units
The **T-bar** unit replaces a single compression bar of length ℓ₀ with an internally tensegritized subassembly: in the cited example, 4 bars and 16 strings forming a class-4 tensegrity. Mass reduction occurs when the internal angle α₁ < 45° (pqac-00000031). The **D-bar** is the dual of the T-bar, obtained by exchanging bars and strings; it is a class-2 tensegrity with string-to-string connections (pqac-00000031). These building blocks enable Skelton's minimum-mass optimization framework.

### 4.2 Minimum-Mass Columns and Plates
Skelton and de Oliveira derive closed-form optimal mass expressions for class-2 tensegrity cylinders parameterized by radius R, half-bay height z, helix angle φ, and complexity q. The normalized mass J = Js + Jb is minimized under material yield constraints, with optimal complexity q* balancing structural efficiency against joint mass penalties (pqac-00000032). For any given aspect ratio ρ and complexity q, the optimal bending angle satisfies tan β* = ρ^(1/q), with asymptotic minimal cost J*∞ = 2 ln ρ⁻¹ as q → ∞ (pqac-00000031).

---

## 5. Tensegrity Domes and Cable-Domes

### 5.1 Geiger Cable-Dome (Seoul Olympic Halls)
David Geiger adapted Fuller's Aspension Dome concept into radial cable-and-strut domes for the Seoul Olympic Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas (1986/1988). These are technically "cable-domes" rather than pure tensegrities because the outer compression ring is not embedded within the cable network (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018). Micheletti and Podio-Guidugli trace the lineage from Fuller's bicycle-wheel-like arrangement through Geiger's implementation (pqac-00000018).

### 5.2 Levy Cable-Dome (Georgia Dome)
Levy revised Geiger's radial layout with a triangulated cable network for the Georgia Dome (1992). Fu's nonlinear FE analysis showed that the primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section, with recommendations to increase prestress in inner cables for enhanced capacity (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). The Georgia Dome used φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires (1670 N/mm²) and Q345 circular tube struts (345 N/mm²) under 0.6 kN/m² uniform roof load (pqac-00000015).

---

## 6. Bio-Inspired and Morphologically Novel Tensegrities

### 6.1 Biotensegrity (Levin, Ingber)
Levin's biotensegrity framework models musculoskeletal structures—spine, shoulder, pelvis—as "continuous tension, discontinuous compression" systems where bones act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Ingber's cellular tensegrity model demonstrates that cells use tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: actin-myosin filaments generate contractile tension (prestress), microtubules serve as compression struts, and intermediate filaments act as guy wires (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). This hierarchical principle operates across scales from single proteins to whole organisms, with mechanotransduction enabled by long-range force transmission through the tensegrity network (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026).

### 6.2 Tensegrity Robots
**NASA SUPERball v1/v2**: A 6-strut icosahedron robot for planetary exploration, featuring 24 spring-cable assemblies and 12 actuators. The v1 (2015) measured ~1.7 m diameter, ~21 kg, with passive cable stiffness ~998 N/m and nominal actuated tension ~250 N (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). SUPERball v2 was redesigned to survive impact velocities upward of 8 m/s with 24 actuators and compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch). The **NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT)** is an open-source simulator built on the Bullet Physics engine, released for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

**Berkeley ULTRA-Spine**: A flexible actuated spine robot using stacked tensegrity vertebra modules, controlled via model-predictive control with inverse statics optimization (pqac-00000007). The TT-3 robot from UC Berkeley is a modular, rod-centered 6-bar tensegrity with distributed actuation and control architecture.

---

## 7. Tensegrity Space Structures and Deployable Systems

### 7.1 Deployable Tensegrity Masts
Tibert and Pellegrino developed deployable tensegrity mast concepts using stacked Snelson-type prisms, investigating both strut-mode deployment for eight-stage masts and tendon-controlled strategies (pqac-00000033). Sultan and Skelton proposed cable-controlled deployment following equilibrium manifolds to maintain structural integrity throughout transformation (pqac-00000034).

### 7.2 Deployable Antenna Patents
**US 6,441,801 B1** (Knight et al., 2002): A screw-motion-driven tensegrity antenna with a parallel-platform architecture consisting of upper hexagonal platform and lower hexagonal base connected by compression strut and tension tie leg pairs (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). **US 6,542,132 B2** (Stern, 2003): A deployable reflector antenna with tensegrity support architecture and mounting frame for improved specific mass and compact stowage (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).

### 7.3 Wave Generation Patent
**US 8,616,328 B2** (Daraio, 2013): A tensegrity apparatus composed of multiple tensegrity units for transmitting solitary waves with adjustable profiles into materials or structures, enabling nondestructive evaluation applications (pqac-00000049).

---

## 8. Tensegrity-Inspired Metamaterials and Additive Manufacturing

### 8.1 Truncated Octahedron Lattices (Rimoli, Pajunen, Bauer)
The truncated-octahedron tensegrity cell (12 struts, 36 cables) is the leading architecture for 3D-printable impact-absorbing metamaterials. Pajunen et al. developed a single-material 3D-printable equivalent validated through ABAQUS simulations, quasi-static compression, and drop-weight impact tests (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030). Bauer et al. achieved unprecedented failure resistance with up to 25-fold deformability enhancement and orders-of-magnitude increased energy absorption through delocalized deformation enabled by compression-member discontinuity (pqac-00000028). Ruffini and Rimoli used graph theory to show that deformation delocalization correlates with asymmetric tension-compression connectivity, providing design principles for failure-resistant metamaterials.

### 8.2 Tunable Tensegrity Tessellations
Liu et al. developed a cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation block (13 struts, 96 cables) with 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms, using polymer-like material properties (E_S = 2600 MPa, E_C = 12 MPa) representative of multi-material 3D printing. Computational homogenization demonstrated rich tunability of effective stiffness and bandgaps (pqac-00000006).

### 8.3 Bistable Tensegrity Units
Intrigila et al. fabricated bistable double-triangular-prism units via stereolithography, demonstrating snap-through behavior with preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000005). Vangelatos et al. extended this to nanoscale using multiphoton lithography with 250 nm minimum feature sizes (pqac-00000041).

### 8.4 Simplex-Based Lattice Metamaterials
Sabouni-Zawadzka systematically compared five regular tensegrity unit cells—4-strut simplex (quasi-bimode), 3-strut simplex (quasi-trimode), expanded octahedron (quasi-trimode), truncated tetrahedron (trimode), and X-module (unimode)—identifying soft and stiff deformation modes via eigenanalysis of equivalent elasticity matrices (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038). Self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio are the primary tuning parameters, with six representative deformation modes: stiff, soft, and medium extensional, plus high (double) and low shear (pqac-00000040).

---

## 9. Topology Generation and Computational Design Methods

### 9.1 Form-Finding Methods
Tibert and Pellegrino's 2003 review established the standard taxonomy of form-finding approaches: force-density methods, energy minimization, dynamic relaxation, and analytical solutions for regular topologies (pqac-00000017). Recent advances include genetic-algorithm-based total potential energy minimization for free-form tensegrities (Uzun 2017) and deep neural networks for form-finding that substitute trained DNNs for eigenvalue decomposition of force-density matrices (Lee et al. 2022). Graph neural networks have also been applied to tensegrity form-finding (Shao et al. 2024).

### 9.2 Open-Source Software
Key open-source tools include: **NTRT (NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit)**, built on the Bullet Physics engine for tensegrity robot simulation (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012); **MOTES (MOdeling TENsegrity Structures)**, a MATLAB-based open-source tool by Skelton's group for statics, dynamics, and form-finding of general tensegrity systems; and various research codes for computational homogenization of tensegrity metamaterials.

### 9.3 Elastic Lattice Patent for Tensegrity Robots
**US 2019/0382995 A1** (Chen, 2019): An elastic lattice platform for rapid prototyping of tensegrity structures and robots, where tensile members form a spatially defined structure without compressive members touching.

---

## 10. Recommendations for BYU Multi-Material 3D-Printed Tensegrity Project

For the BYU Mentored Research Grant project targeting impact-absorbing crutch tips and energy-absorbing lattices using PETG struts + TPU tendons on a Bambu Lab H2D printer, the following table ranks the most promising starting geometries:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key Rationale and Parameter Recommendations

**Top Priority: Truncated Octahedron Cell (Rank 1).** This cell has the strongest experimental validation for impact absorption (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Its 12-strut/36-cable topology maps naturally to PETG compression members and TPU tension members. The Bambu H2D's multi-material capability can print PETG struts with TPU tendons in a single build, potentially eliminating post-assembly. Critical design variables for Bayesian optimization include: unit-cell edge length (5–20 mm), strut diameter (0.8–3 mm), TPU tendon diameter (0.4–1.5 mm), initial tendon prestrain (0–10%), node fillet radius, and lattice relative density (5–30%).

**Calibration Benchmark: T3 Simplex (Rank 2).** The 3-bar prism (3 struts, 9 cables, 6 nodes) is the ideal calibration geometry because it has a single self-stress state and single mechanism, enabling clean validation of PETG/TPU constitutive models and the prestress-printing workflow before scaling to more complex cells (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036).

**Stacked Prismatic Column (Rank 7).** Particularly suited to the crutch-tip application because its axial geometry matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios. Progressive bay collapse/twisting under axial impact can absorb energy through multiple stages, and functionally graded stiffness along the column height can be achieved by varying bay parameters.

**Material-Specific Parameters for Bayesian Optimization:**
- **PETG struts**: diameter (0.8–4 mm), wall thickness if hollow (0.4–1.2 mm), length/slenderness ratio (critical for Euler buckling plateau)
- **TPU tendons**: durometer (80A–95A), cross-section (0.4–2 mm diameter), initial stretch/prestrain (0–15%)

**Open-Source Resources:** The NASA NTRT simulator (open-source, GitHub) provides validated physics for tensegrity dynamics. MOTES (MATLAB open-source by Skelton's group) handles statics and form-finding. For CAD generation, the parametric geometry of all recommended cells can be scripted in Python/OpenSCAD from published node coordinates. The Pajunen/Rimoli truncated-octahedron cell geometry is fully specified in the literature and reproducible for STL generation (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

---

## 11. Conclusion

This survey documents the remarkable breadth of tensegrity structural designs spanning seven decades—from Snelson's original prismatic sculptures through NASA's SUPERball planetary lander to Rimoli's failure-resistant metamaterials. For the BYU multi-material 3D-printing project, the truncated-octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell emerges as the highest-priority starting geometry due to its validated impact performance, space-tileability, and natural compatibility with PETG-strut/TPU-tendon multi-material fabrication (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). The 3-bar simplex provides the ideal calibration benchmark (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036), while the 4-strut simplex and expanded octahedron offer rich intermediate complexity for parametric exploration (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). Bistable double-prism units add snap-through energy absorption capabilities particularly suited to crutch-tip applications (pqac-00000036). The stacked prismatic column geometry most naturally matches the axial loading profile of a crutch tip (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018). All recommended geometries have sufficient published geometric specifications for parametric CAD generation, and the rich design variable space—spanning strut/tendon dimensions, prestrain, cell count, grading, and material selection—is well-suited to Bayesian optimization for systematic performance improvement."}

Tensegrity ("tensional integrity") structures comprise isolated compression members (struts/bars) suspended within a continuous network of tension members (cables/tendons), achieving self-equilibrium through internal prestress. Since Kenneth Snelson's 1948 X-piece sculpture and R. ---

## 2. Canonical Snelson-Class Prismatic Tensegrities

### 2.1 Three-Bar Prism (T3 / Simplex)
The simplest true tensegrity is the 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3): 3 struts, 9 cables (minimal) or 12 cables (non-minimal), and 6 nodes. Two triangular end-polygons are connected by struts with a characteristic stable twist angle θ = π/2 − π/n; for n = 3, θ = 30° (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2, oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40). The T3 possesses one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent self-stress state; the mechanism is a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases, stabilized by the self-stress (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4). Oliveira and Skelton present this as the foundational "regular minimal tensegrity prism," noting that non-minimal variants with 12 strings provide higher stiffness and eliminate soft modes (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40).

### 2.2 Four-Bar Prism (T4 / 4-Strut Simplex)
The 4-strut simplex consists of 4 struts and 12 cables arranged in an 8-node prism with one base rotated 135° relative to the other. Sabouni-Zawadzka and Gilewski classify it as a "quasi-bimode" extreme metamaterial unit cell, featuring stiff, soft, and medium extensional modes plus high and low shear modes. The self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio serve as primary tuning parameters (sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 3-4, sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 1-3).

### 2.3 Higher-Order Prisms and Stacked Columns
The n-bar prism family generalizes to T6 (θ = 60°) and beyond. Prism twist angles cluster near 30–36° with cable pretension in the 1.8–2.5% engineering strain range for typical designs (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2). Snelson's iconic Needle Tower I (1968) and Needle Tower II (1969) are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms to form columnar masts (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). Yildiz and Lesieutre developed effective continuum beam stiffness properties for n-strut cylindrical tensegrity towers, enabling homogenized analysis of long stacked-prism columns for space applications.

---

## 3. Polyhedral / Spherical Tensegrities

### 3.1 Six-Strut Tensegrity Icosahedron
The 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (also called Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron) is the canonical spherical tensegrity: 6 struts and 24 cables. This topology forms the basis of the NASA SUPERball robot, where the 2015 prototype featured 1.7 m struts, ~21 kg mass, 24 spring-cable assemblies, and 12 BLDC actuators (sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 1-2, sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 80-83). A payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies for payload suspension (sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 29-32).

### 3.2 Expanded Octahedron
The expanded octahedron tensegrity has been studied as a metamaterial unit cell exhibiting three stiff modes, one purely soft mode, and two quasi-soft modes, with the largest positive-definite elasticity region among five compared regular tensegrity modules (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17). Vangelatos et al. fabricated expanded-octahedron-based bistable lattices using multiphoton lithography at nanoscale (minimum strut radii ~250 nm), demonstrating preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (vangelatos2020designandtesting pages 1-3).

### 3.3 Truncated Tetrahedron
The truncated tetrahedron module is identified as the most "extreme" regular tensegrity unit cell, featuring three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes (classified as a "trimode" material). However, its required self-stress and stiffness ranges lie beyond current practical fabrication limits (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 1-3).

### 3.4 Truncated Octahedron (Rimoli Cell)
The truncated octahedron tensegrity cell, introduced by Rimoli and Pal, has 12 struts and 36 cables and is inherently space-tileable. This cell is the foundation of the most important recent work on tensegrity metamaterials. Bauer et al. demonstrated that recursive reflection of truncated-octahedron cells into 2×2×2 and larger supercells creates metamaterials with isolated compression-member loops, suppressing localized failure and achieving up to 25-fold enhancement in deformability and orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption relative to same-strength conventional lattice architectures (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Pajunen et al. developed a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity with post-buckling stability and load-limiting behavior, validated through both quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact experiments (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2).

---

## 4. Class-k Tensegrities

Skelton defines a "class-k" tensegrity as one in which at most k rigid bodies share a node. Class-1 tensegrities have no strut-to-strut connections (the canonical definition), while higher classes permit shared nodes (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62, oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 98-111).

### 4.1 T-Bar and D-Bar Units
The **T-bar** unit replaces a single compression bar of length ℓ₀ with an internally tensegritized subassembly: in the cited example, 4 bars and 16 strings forming a class-4 tensegrity. Mass reduction occurs when the internal angle α₁ < 45° (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62). The **D-bar** is the dual of the T-bar, obtained by exchanging bars and strings; it is a class-2 tensegrity with string-to-string connections (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62). These building blocks enable Skelton's minimum-mass optimization framework.

### 4.2 Minimum-Mass Columns and Plates
Skelton and de Oliveira derive closed-form optimal mass expressions for class-2 tensegrity cylinders parameterized by radius R, half-bay height z, helix angle φ, and complexity q. The normalized mass J = Js + Jb is minimized under material yield constraints, with optimal complexity q* balancing structural efficiency against joint mass penalties (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 98-111). For any given aspect ratio ρ and complexity q, the optimal bending angle satisfies tan β* = ρ^(1/q), with asymptotic minimal cost J*∞ = 2 ln ρ⁻¹ as q → ∞ (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62).

---

## 5. Tensegrity Domes and Cable-Domes

### 5.1 Geiger Cable-Dome (Seoul Olympic Halls)
David Geiger adapted Fuller's Aspension Dome concept into radial cable-and-strut domes for the Seoul Olympic Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas (1986/1988). These are technically "cable-domes" rather than pure tensegrities because the outer compression ring is not embedded within the cable network (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 1-4, micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). Micheletti and Podio-Guidugli trace the lineage from Fuller's bicycle-wheel-like arrangement through Geiger's implementation (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6).

### 5.2 Levy Cable-Dome (Georgia Dome)
Levy revised Geiger's radial layout with a triangulated cable network for the Georgia Dome (1992). Fu's nonlinear FE analysis showed that the primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section, with recommendations to increase prestress in inner cables for enhanced capacity (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 4-9, fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 9-13). The Georgia Dome used φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires (1670 N/mm²) and Q345 circular tube struts (345 N/mm²) under 0.6 kN/m² uniform roof load (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 4-9).

---

## 6. Bio-Inspired and Morphologically Novel Tensegrities

### 6.1 Biotensegrity (Levin, Ingber)
Levin's biotensegrity framework models musculoskeletal structures—spine, shoulder, pelvis—as "continuous tension, discontinuous compression" systems where bones act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network (levin2007chapter15– pages 9-9, scarr2020biotensegritywhatis pages 1-2). Ingber's cellular tensegrity model demonstrates that cells use tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: actin-myosin filaments generate contractile tension (prestress), microtubules serve as compression struts, and intermediate filaments act as guy wires (swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 4-6, ingber2008tensegritybasedmechanosensingfrom pages 5-7, ingber2008tensegritybasedmechanosensingfrom pages 9-10, ingber2014tensegritycellularbiophysics pages 1-3). This hierarchical principle operates across scales from single proteins to whole organisms, with mechanotransduction enabled by long-range force transmission through the tensegrity network (swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 6-8, swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 2-4).

### 6.2 Tensegrity Robots
**NASA SUPERball v1/v2**: A 6-strut icosahedron robot for planetary exploration, featuring 24 spring-cable assemblies and 12 actuators. The v1 (2015) measured ~1.7 m diameter, ~21 kg, with passive cable stiffness ~998 N/m and nominal actuated tension ~250 N (sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 1-2, sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 80-83). SUPERball v2 was redesigned to survive impact velocities upward of 8 m/s with 24 actuators and compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch). The **NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT)** is an open-source simulator built on the Bullet Physics engine, released for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies (sabelhaus2014hardwaredesignand pages 1-2, sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 2-3).

**Berkeley ULTRA-Spine**: A flexible actuated spine robot using stacked tensegrity vertebra modules, controlled via model-predictive control with inverse statics optimization (sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 29-32). The TT-3 robot from UC Berkeley is a modular, rod-centered 6-bar tensegrity with distributed actuation and control architecture.

---

## 7. Tensegrity Space Structures and Deployable Systems

### 7.1 Deployable Tensegrity Masts
Tibert and Pellegrino developed deployable tensegrity mast concepts using stacked Snelson-type prisms, investigating both strut-mode deployment for eight-stage masts and tendon-controlled strategies (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 21-23). Sultan and Skelton proposed cable-controlled deployment following equilibrium manifolds to maintain structural integrity throughout transformation (rhodebarbarigos2012anactivedeployable pages 34-37).

### 7.2 Deployable Antenna Patents
**US 6,441,801 B1** (Knight et al., 2002): A screw-motion-driven tensegrity antenna with a parallel-platform architecture consisting of upper hexagonal platform and lower hexagonal base connected by compression strut and tension tie leg pairs (US6441801B1 pages 2-9, US6441801B1 pages 9-10, US6441801B1 pages 1-2). **US 6,542,132 B2** (Stern, 2003): A deployable reflector antenna with tensegrity support architecture and mounting frame for improved specific mass and compact stowage (US6542132B2 pages 1-9, US6542132B2 pages 9-10).

### 7.3 Wave Generation Patent
**US 8,616,328 B2** (Daraio, 2013): A tensegrity apparatus composed of multiple tensegrity units for transmitting solitary waves with adjustable profiles into materials or structures, enabling nondestructive evaluation applications (US8616328B2 pages 1-2).

---

## 8. Tensegrity-Inspired Metamaterials and Additive Manufacturing

### 8.1 Truncated Octahedron Lattices (Rimoli, Pajunen, Bauer)
The truncated-octahedron tensegrity cell (12 struts, 36 cables) is the leading architecture for 3D-printable impact-absorbing metamaterials. Pajunen et al. developed a single-material 3D-printable equivalent validated through ABAQUS simulations, quasi-static compression, and drop-weight impact tests (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2). Bauer et al. achieved unprecedented failure resistance with up to 25-fold deformability enhancement and orders-of-magnitude increased energy absorption through delocalized deformation enabled by compression-member discontinuity (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Ruffini and Rimoli used graph theory to show that deformation delocalization correlates with asymmetric tension-compression connectivity, providing design principles for failure-resistant metamaterials.

### 8.2 Tunable Tensegrity Tessellations
Liu et al. developed a cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation block (13 struts, 96 cables) with 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms, using polymer-like material properties (E_S = 2600 MPa, E_C = 12 MPa) representative of multi-material 3D printing. Computational homogenization demonstrated rich tunability of effective stiffness and bandgaps (liu2019unravelingtensegritytessellations pages 7-9).

### 8.3 Bistable Tensegrity Units
Intrigila et al. fabricated bistable double-triangular-prism units via stereolithography, demonstrating snap-through behavior with preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 12-12). Vangelatos et al. extended this to nanoscale using multiphoton lithography with 250 nm minimum feature sizes (vangelatos2020designandtesting pages 1-3).

### 8.4 Simplex-Based Lattice Metamaterials
Sabouni-Zawadzka systematically compared five regular tensegrity unit cells—4-strut simplex (quasi-bimode), 3-strut simplex (quasi-trimode), expanded octahedron (quasi-trimode), truncated tetrahedron (trimode), and X-module (unimode)—identifying soft and stiff deformation modes via eigenanalysis of equivalent elasticity matrices (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 1-3). Self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio are the primary tuning parameters, with six representative deformation modes: stiff, soft, and medium extensional, plus high (double) and low shear (sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 1-3).

---

## 9. Topology Generation and Computational Design Methods

### 9.1 Form-Finding Methods
Tibert and Pellegrino's 2003 review established the standard taxonomy of form-finding approaches: force-density methods, energy minimization, dynamic relaxation, and analytical solutions for regular topologies (uzun2017formfindingandanalysis pages 1-2). Recent advances include genetic-algorithm-based total potential energy minimization for free-form tensegrities (Uzun 2017) and deep neural networks for form-finding that substitute trained DNNs for eigenvalue decomposition of force-density matrices (Lee et al. 2022). Graph neural networks have also been applied to tensegrity form-finding (Shao et al. 2024).

### 9.2 Open-Source Software
Key open-source tools include: **NTRT (NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit)**, built on the Bullet Physics engine for tensegrity robot simulation (sabelhaus2014hardwaredesignand pages 1-2, sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 2-3); **MOTES (MOdeling TENsegrity Structures)**, a MATLAB-based open-source tool by Skelton's group for statics, dynamics, and form-finding of general tensegrity systems; and various research codes for computational homogenization of tensegrity metamaterials.

### 9.3 Elastic Lattice Patent for Tensegrity Robots
**US 2019/0382995 A1** (Chen, 2019): An elastic lattice platform for rapid prototyping of tensegrity structures and robots, where tensile members form a spatially defined structure without compressive members touching.

---

### Key Rationale and Parameter Recommendations

**Top Priority: Truncated Octahedron Cell (Rank 1).** This cell has the strongest experimental validation for impact absorption (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Its 12-strut/36-cable topology maps naturally to PETG compression members and TPU tension members. The Bambu H2D's multi-material capability can print PETG struts with TPU tendons in a single build, potentially eliminating post-assembly. Critical design variables for Bayesian optimization include: unit-cell edge length (5–20 mm), strut diameter (0.8–3 mm), TPU tendon diameter (0.4–1.5 mm), initial tendon prestrain (0–10%), node fillet radius, and lattice relative density (5–30%).

**Calibration Benchmark: T3 Simplex (Rank 2).** The 3-bar prism (3 struts, 9 cables, 6 nodes) is the ideal calibration geometry because it has a single self-stress state and single mechanism, enabling clean validation of PETG/TPU constitutive models and the prestress-printing workflow before scaling to more complex cells (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4).

**Stacked Prismatic Column (Rank 7).** Particularly suited to the crutch-tip application because its axial geometry matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios. Progressive bay collapse/twisting under axial impact can absorb energy through multiple stages, and functionally graded stiffness along the column height can be achieved by varying bay parameters.

**Material-Specific Parameters for Bayesian Optimization:**
- **PETG struts**: diameter (0.8–4 mm), wall thickness if hollow (0.4–1.2 mm), length/slenderness ratio (critical for Euler buckling plateau)
- **TPU tendons**: durometer (80A–95A), cross-section (0.4–2 mm diameter), initial stretch/prestrain (0–15%)
- **Interface**: node geometry/fillet radius, PETG-TPU bonding area, overhang angle constraints
- **Lattice-level**: cell count per axis (2×2×2 to 6×6×6), grading function, boundary/skin conditions, overall relative density

**Open-Source Resources:** The NASA NTRT simulator (open-source, GitHub) provides validated physics for tensegrity dynamics. MOTES (MATLAB open-source by Skelton's group) handles statics and form-finding. For CAD generation, the parametric geometry of all recommended cells can be scripted in Python/OpenSCAD from published node coordinates. The Pajunen/Rimoli truncated-octahedron cell geometry is fully specified in the literature and reproducible for STL generation (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, liu2019unravelingtensegritytessellations pages 7-9).

---

## 11. Conclusion

This survey documents the remarkable breadth of tensegrity structural designs spanning seven decades—from Snelson's original prismatic sculptures through NASA's SUPERball planetary lander to Rimoli's failure-resistant metamaterials. For the BYU multi-material 3D-printing project, the truncated-octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell emerges as the highest-priority starting geometry due to its validated impact performance, space-tileability, and natural compatibility with PETG-strut/TPU-tendon multi-material fabrication (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). The 3-bar simplex provides the ideal calibration benchmark (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4), while the 4-strut simplex and expanded octahedron offer rich intermediate complexity for parametric exploration (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 3-4). Bistable double-prism units add snap-through energy absorption capabilities particularly suited to crutch-tip applications (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4). The stacked prismatic column geometry most naturally matches the axial loading profile of a crutch tip (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2, micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). All recommended geometries have sufficient published geometric specifications for parametric CAD generation, and the rich design variable space—spanning strut/tendon dimensions, prestrain, cell count, grading, and material selection—is well-suited to Bayesian optimization for systematic performance improvement.

Tensegrity ("tensional integrity") structures comprise isolated compression members (struts/bars) suspended within a continuous network of tension members (cables/tendons), achieving self-equilibrium through internal prestress. Since Kenneth Snelson's 1948 X-piece sculpture and R. ## 2. Canonical Snelson-Class Prismatic Tensegrities

### 2.1 Three-Bar Prism (T3 / Simplex)
The simplest true tensegrity is the 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3): 3 struts, 9 cables (minimal) or 12 cables (non-minimal), and 6 nodes. Two triangular end-polygons are connected by struts with a characteristic stable twist angle θ = π/2 − π/n; for n = 3, θ = 30° (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). The T3 possesses one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent self-stress state; the mechanism is a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases, stabilized by the self-stress (pqac-00000036). Oliveira and Skelton present this as the foundational "regular minimal tensegrity prism," noting that non-minimal variants with 12 strings provide higher stiffness and eliminate soft modes (pqac-00000001).

### 2.2 Four-Bar Prism (T4 / 4-Strut Simplex)
The 4-strut simplex consists of 4 struts and 12 cables arranged in an 8-node prism with one base rotated 135° relative to the other. Sabouni-Zawadzka and Gilewski classify it as a "quasi-bimode" extreme metamaterial unit cell, featuring stiff, soft, and medium extensional modes plus high and low shear modes. The self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio serve as primary tuning parameters (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040).

### 2.3 Higher-Order Prisms and Stacked Columns
The n-bar prism family generalizes to T6 (θ = 60°) and beyond. Prism twist angles cluster near 30–36° with cable pretension in the 1.8–2.5% engineering strain range for typical designs (pqac-00000000). Snelson's iconic Needle Tower I (1968) and Needle Tower II (1969) are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms to form columnar masts (pqac-00000018). Yildiz and Lesieutre developed effective continuum beam stiffness properties for n-strut cylindrical tensegrity towers, enabling homogenized analysis of long stacked-prism columns for space applications.

## 3. Polyhedral / Spherical Tensegrities

### 3.1 Six-Strut Tensegrity Icosahedron
The 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (also called Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron) is the canonical spherical tensegrity: 6 struts and 24 cables. This topology forms the basis of the NASA SUPERball robot, where the 2015 prototype featured 1.7 m struts, ~21 kg mass, 24 spring-cable assemblies, and 12 BLDC actuators (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). A payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies for payload suspension (pqac-00000007).

### 3.2 Expanded Octahedron
The expanded octahedron tensegrity has been studied as a metamaterial unit cell exhibiting three stiff modes, one purely soft mode, and two quasi-soft modes, with the largest positive-definite elasticity region among five compared regular tensegrity modules (pqac-00000035). Vangelatos et al. fabricated expanded-octahedron-based bistable lattices using multiphoton lithography at nanoscale (minimum strut radii ~250 nm), demonstrating preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000041).

### 3.3 Truncated Tetrahedron
The truncated tetrahedron module is identified as the most "extreme" regular tensegrity unit cell, featuring three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes (classified as a "trimode" material). However, its required self-stress and stiffness ranges lie beyond current practical fabrication limits (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038).

### 3.4 Truncated Octahedron (Rimoli Cell)
The truncated octahedron tensegrity cell, introduced by Rimoli and Pal, has 12 struts and 36 cables and is inherently space-tileable. This cell is the foundation of the most important recent work on tensegrity metamaterials. Bauer et al. demonstrated that recursive reflection of truncated-octahedron cells into 2×2×2 and larger supercells creates metamaterials with isolated compression-member loops, suppressing localized failure and achieving up to 25-fold enhancement in deformability and orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption relative to same-strength conventional lattice architectures (pqac-00000028). Pajunen et al. developed a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity with post-buckling stability and load-limiting behavior, validated through both quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact experiments (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030).

## 4. Class-k Tensegrities

Skelton defines a "class-k" tensegrity as one in which at most k rigid bodies share a node. Class-1 tensegrities have no strut-to-strut connections (the canonical definition), while higher classes permit shared nodes (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

### 4.1 T-Bar and D-Bar Units
The **T-bar** unit replaces a single compression bar of length ℓ₀ with an internally tensegritized subassembly: in the cited example, 4 bars and 16 strings forming a class-4 tensegrity. Mass reduction occurs when the internal angle α₁ < 45° (pqac-00000031). The **D-bar** is the dual of the T-bar, obtained by exchanging bars and strings; it is a class-2 tensegrity with string-to-string connections (pqac-00000031). These building blocks enable Skelton's minimum-mass optimization framework.

### 4.2 Minimum-Mass Columns and Plates
Skelton and de Oliveira derive closed-form optimal mass expressions for class-2 tensegrity cylinders parameterized by radius R, half-bay height z, helix angle φ, and complexity q. The normalized mass J = Js + Jb is minimized under material yield constraints, with optimal complexity q* balancing structural efficiency against joint mass penalties (pqac-00000032). For any given aspect ratio ρ and complexity q, the optimal bending angle satisfies tan β* = ρ^(1/q), with asymptotic minimal cost J*∞ = 2 ln ρ⁻¹ as q → ∞ (pqac-00000031).

## 5. Tensegrity Domes and Cable-Domes

### 5.1 Geiger Cable-Dome (Seoul Olympic Halls)
David Geiger adapted Fuller's Aspension Dome concept into radial cable-and-strut domes for the Seoul Olympic Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas (1986/1988). These are technically "cable-domes" rather than pure tensegrities because the outer compression ring is not embedded within the cable network (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018). Micheletti and Podio-Guidugli trace the lineage from Fuller's bicycle-wheel-like arrangement through Geiger's implementation (pqac-00000018).

### 5.2 Levy Cable-Dome (Georgia Dome)
Levy revised Geiger's radial layout with a triangulated cable network for the Georgia Dome (1992). Fu's nonlinear FE analysis showed that the primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section, with recommendations to increase prestress in inner cables for enhanced capacity (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). The Georgia Dome used φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires (1670 N/mm²) and Q345 circular tube struts (345 N/mm²) under 0.6 kN/m² uniform roof load (pqac-00000015).

## 6. Bio-Inspired and Morphologically Novel Tensegrities

### 6.1 Biotensegrity (Levin, Ingber)
Levin's biotensegrity framework models musculoskeletal structures—spine, shoulder, pelvis—as "continuous tension, discontinuous compression" systems where bones act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Ingber's cellular tensegrity model demonstrates that cells use tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: actin-myosin filaments generate contractile tension (prestress), microtubules serve as compression struts, and intermediate filaments act as guy wires (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). This hierarchical principle operates across scales from single proteins to whole organisms, with mechanotransduction enabled by long-range force transmission through the tensegrity network (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026).

### 6.2 Tensegrity Robots
**NASA SUPERball v1/v2**: A 6-strut icosahedron robot for planetary exploration, featuring 24 spring-cable assemblies and 12 actuators. The v1 (2015) measured ~1.7 m diameter, ~21 kg, with passive cable stiffness ~998 N/m and nominal actuated tension ~250 N (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). SUPERball v2 was redesigned to survive impact velocities upward of 8 m/s with 24 actuators and compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch). The **NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT)** is an open-source simulator built on the Bullet Physics engine, released for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

**Berkeley ULTRA-Spine**: A flexible actuated spine robot using stacked tensegrity vertebra modules, controlled via model-predictive control with inverse statics optimization (pqac-00000007). The TT-3 robot from UC Berkeley is a modular, rod-centered 6-bar tensegrity with distributed actuation and control architecture.

## 7. Tensegrity Space Structures and Deployable Systems

### 7.1 Deployable Tensegrity Masts
Tibert and Pellegrino developed deployable tensegrity mast concepts using stacked Snelson-type prisms, investigating both strut-mode deployment for eight-stage masts and tendon-controlled strategies (pqac-00000033). Sultan and Skelton proposed cable-controlled deployment following equilibrium manifolds to maintain structural integrity throughout transformation (pqac-00000034).

### 7.2 Deployable Antenna Patents
**US 6,441,801 B1** (Knight et al., 2002): A screw-motion-driven tensegrity antenna with a parallel-platform architecture consisting of upper hexagonal platform and lower hexagonal base connected by compression strut and tension tie leg pairs (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). **US 6,542,132 B2** (Stern, 2003): A deployable reflector antenna with tensegrity support architecture and mounting frame for improved specific mass and compact stowage (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).

### 7.3 Wave Generation Patent
**US 8,616,328 B2** (Daraio, 2013): A tensegrity apparatus composed of multiple tensegrity units for transmitting solitary waves with adjustable profiles into materials or structures, enabling nondestructive evaluation applications (pqac-00000049).

## 8. Tensegrity-Inspired Metamaterials and Additive Manufacturing

### 8.1 Truncated Octahedron Lattices (Rimoli, Pajunen, Bauer)
The truncated-octahedron tensegrity cell (12 struts, 36 cables) is the leading architecture for 3D-printable impact-absorbing metamaterials. Pajunen et al. developed a single-material 3D-printable equivalent validated through ABAQUS simulations, quasi-static compression, and drop-weight impact tests (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030). Bauer et al. achieved unprecedented failure resistance with up to 25-fold deformability enhancement and orders-of-magnitude increased energy absorption through delocalized deformation enabled by compression-member discontinuity (pqac-00000028). Ruffini and Rimoli used graph theory to show that deformation delocalization correlates with asymmetric tension-compression connectivity, providing design principles for failure-resistant metamaterials.

### 8.2 Tunable Tensegrity Tessellations
Liu et al. developed a cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation block (13 struts, 96 cables) with 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms, using polymer-like material properties (E_S = 2600 MPa, E_C = 12 MPa) representative of multi-material 3D printing. Computational homogenization demonstrated rich tunability of effective stiffness and bandgaps (pqac-00000006).

### 8.3 Bistable Tensegrity Units
Intrigila et al. fabricated bistable double-triangular-prism units via stereolithography, demonstrating snap-through behavior with preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000005). Vangelatos et al. extended this to nanoscale using multiphoton lithography with 250 nm minimum feature sizes (pqac-00000041).

### 8.4 Simplex-Based Lattice Metamaterials
Sabouni-Zawadzka systematically compared five regular tensegrity unit cells—4-strut simplex (quasi-bimode), 3-strut simplex (quasi-trimode), expanded octahedron (quasi-trimode), truncated tetrahedron (trimode), and X-module (unimode)—identifying soft and stiff deformation modes via eigenanalysis of equivalent elasticity matrices (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000038). Self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio are the primary tuning parameters, with six representative deformation modes: stiff, soft, and medium extensional, plus high (double) and low shear (pqac-00000040).

## 9. Topology Generation and Computational Design Methods

### 9.1 Form-Finding Methods
Tibert and Pellegrino's 2003 review established the standard taxonomy of form-finding approaches: force-density methods, energy minimization, dynamic relaxation, and analytical solutions for regular topologies (pqac-00000017). Recent advances include genetic-algorithm-based total potential energy minimization for free-form tensegrities (Uzun 2017) and deep neural networks for form-finding that substitute trained DNNs for eigenvalue decomposition of force-density matrices (Lee et al. 2022). Graph neural networks have also been applied to tensegrity form-finding (Shao et al. 2024).

### 9.2 Open-Source Software
Key open-source tools include: **NTRT (NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit)**, built on the Bullet Physics engine for tensegrity robot simulation (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012); **MOTES (MOdeling TENsegrity Structures)**, a MATLAB-based open-source tool by Skelton's group for statics, dynamics, and form-finding of general tensegrity systems; and various research codes for computational homogenization of tensegrity metamaterials.

### 9.3 Elastic Lattice Patent for Tensegrity Robots
**US 2019/0382995 A1** (Chen, 2019): An elastic lattice platform for rapid prototyping of tensegrity structures and robots, where tensile members form a spatially defined structure without compressive members touching.

### Key Rationale and Parameter Recommendations

**Top Priority: Truncated Octahedron Cell (Rank 1).** This cell has the strongest experimental validation for impact absorption (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). Its 12-strut/36-cable topology maps naturally to PETG compression members and TPU tension members. The Bambu H2D's multi-material capability can print PETG struts with TPU tendons in a single build, potentially eliminating post-assembly. Critical design variables for Bayesian optimization include: unit-cell edge length (5–20 mm), strut diameter (0.8–3 mm), TPU tendon diameter (0.4–1.5 mm), initial tendon prestrain (0–10%), node fillet radius, and lattice relative density (5–30%).

**Calibration Benchmark: T3 Simplex (Rank 2).** The 3-bar prism (3 struts, 9 cables, 6 nodes) is the ideal calibration geometry because it has a single self-stress state and single mechanism, enabling clean validation of PETG/TPU constitutive models and the prestress-printing workflow before scaling to more complex cells (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036).

**Stacked Prismatic Column (Rank 7).** Particularly suited to the crutch-tip application because its axial geometry matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios. Progressive bay collapse/twisting under axial impact can absorb energy through multiple stages, and functionally graded stiffness along the column height can be achieved by varying bay parameters.

**Material-Specific Parameters for Bayesian Optimization:**
- **PETG struts**: diameter (0.8–4 mm), wall thickness if hollow (0.4–1.2 mm), length/slenderness ratio (critical for Euler buckling plateau)
- **TPU tendons**: durometer (80A–95A), cross-section (0.4–2 mm diameter), initial stretch/prestrain (0–15%)
- **Interface**: node geometry/fillet radius, PETG-TPU bonding area, overhang angle constraints
- **Lattice-level**: cell count per axis (2×2×2 to 6×6×6), grading function, boundary/skin conditions, overall relative density

**Open-Source Resources:** The NASA NTRT simulator (open-source, GitHub) provides validated physics for tensegrity dynamics. MOTES (MATLAB open-source by Skelton's group) handles statics and form-finding. For CAD generation, the parametric geometry of all recommended cells can be scripted in Python/OpenSCAD from published node coordinates. The Pajunen/Rimoli truncated-octahedron cell geometry is fully specified in the literature and reproducible for STL generation (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

## 11. Conclusion

This survey documents the remarkable breadth of tensegrity structural designs spanning seven decades—from Snelson's original prismatic sculptures through NASA's SUPERball planetary lander to Rimoli's failure-resistant metamaterials. For the BYU multi-material 3D-printing project, the truncated-octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell emerges as the highest-priority starting geometry due to its validated impact performance, space-tileability, and natural compatibility with PETG-strut/TPU-tendon multi-material fabrication (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). The 3-bar simplex provides the ideal calibration benchmark (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036), while the 4-strut simplex and expanded octahedron offer rich intermediate complexity for parametric exploration (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). Bistable double-prism units add snap-through energy absorption capabilities particularly suited to crutch-tip applications (pqac-00000036). The stacked prismatic column geometry most naturally matches the axial loading profile of a crutch tip (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018). All recommended geometries have sufficient published geometric specifications for parametric CAD generation, and the rich design variable space—spanning strut/tendon dimensions, prestrain, cell count, grading, and material selection—is well-suited to Bayesian optimization for systematic performance improvement.

snippets: tensegrity systems are a special class of spatial reticulated structures that are composed of struts and cables.

The most recent and widely accepted definition was proposed in 2003 by Motro: “A tensegrity is a system in stable self-equilibrated state comprising a discontinuous set of compressed components  inside a continuum  of tensioned components”.
Skelton et al. (2001) proposed the term “Class k” to distinguish the different types of systems
A “Class k” tensegrity system is defined as a stable tensegrity system with a maximum of k interconnected compressive members.
A key step in the design of tensegrity structures  is the determination of a self-stressed geometrical configuration. This step is known as form-finding or prestressability problem.

The number of self-stress states s in a system is given by:

                                  s = b − rA
Conform self-stress states have all struts in compression and all cables in tension (Quirant, Kazi-Aoual et al. 2003).

The number of internal mechanisms m in a reticulated system is given by:

                  m = N − rA

contexts.context: The excerpt describes prismatic tensegrities (T-prisms) in terms of node-based kinematics and equilibrium. A tensegrity prism has 2p nodes (DoF = 3(2p) before constraints) and the T-prism consists of p bar elements. Constraints reduce degrees of freedom: DoF = 6p − nc when nc constraints are applied. Geometric parameters br, tr, p, ph and twist angle α define the prism; the characteristic polygon angle is φ = 2π/p. Node positions are generated by repeatedly applying a rotation matrix R(φ) (i being the rotation index) to produce bottom and top node sets; all nodes are assembled in a node matrix N. Form-finding and equilibrium are expressed compactly in node space via the force-density formulation W = N C^T Q C and the equilibrium NC^T Q C − F = 0. Holonomic constraints are written as Gk(N) = Nij − Nij(0) = 0 and enforced via Lagrange multipliers Λk. The excerpt provides the mathematical framework for generating T-prism geometries, applying twist-angle bounds (α stated in the text), and performing form-finding using node-based force-density plus constraint enforcement.

snippets: Experimental investigations on mechanical properties of 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired metamaterials.
This paper presents results of uniaxial compression tests carried out on a number of 3D-printed tensegrity-based modules
diﬀering in the manufacturing technology, the parent material, and the cell size.

one of the most important parameters that has a direct impact on the results is the elongation at break of the parent material; any inaccuracies at the production stage greatly aﬀect the mechanical behaviour of the structure; it is crucial to ensure a free deformation consistent with the inﬁnitesimal mechanism mode of tensegrity; a post-critical behaviour of the struts was clearly visible in the performed tests.
Tensegrity metamaterials were proposed for the ﬁrst time by Fraternali et al. [10]
A new method for creating 3D tensegrity lattices from truncated octahedron cells was proposed by Rimoli and Pal [14] and extended by Salahsoor et al. [15].
Ma et al. [19] investigated tensegrity systems with metal rubber-based struts, exhibiting good energy absorption and tuneable dynamic properties.

Tensegrity systems have many advantageous features, such as: light weight, high stiﬀness-to-mass ratio, controllability, inherent attributes of smart structures, free geometry shaping, and unique mechanical properties.

contexts.context: Pages 1–3 introduce tensegrity-based metamaterials and key concepts relevant to their mechanical behavior. Tensegrities are ‘‘cable-strut systems with a special configuration of nodes’’ that display infinitesimal mechanisms stabilized by self-stress states; occurrence of self-stress means internal forces exist independently of external loads. These properties give tensegrity lattices useful smart features (self-control, self-diagnosis, self-repair and self-adjustment) and practical advantages such as high stiffness-to-mass ratio, controllability, reliability and deployability. Crucially, their static and dynamic response can be tuned by adjusting pre-stress (pre-stressing forces) and by changing member properties (e.g., cable-to-strut stiffness ratio). The paper frames analysis through a continuum model that equates discrete tensegrity strain energy to an equivalent elasticity matrix E; the study of ‘‘extreme materials’’ uses eigenvalues/eigenvectors of this elasticity tensor to classify modes (nullmode, unimode, etc.). The authors note prior results on tunable dynamic response and energy-absorption enhancements (e.g., introducing metal rubber in struts) and mention three representative lattices based on 4-strut simplex modules. The excerpt does not provide details on 3D multi-material printing (PETG/TPU) or specific experimental impact-absorption data by Pajunen, Rimoli, Fraternali, or others.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports medium-scale experimental tests on 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired single-module cells (4‑strut simplex modules). Testing was done in two series: the first compared additive manufacturing (AM) techniques and parent materials; the second examined parent-material influence and scale effects. Three AM methods were evaluated: SLA, SLS, and PolyJet (modified SLA); SLS was rejected early due to brittle parent-material behavior. Modules were printed at sizes determined by manufacturer limits (cells inscribed in 20–50 mm cubes), with the authors noting that realistic metamaterials should be micro- or nano-scale but were not feasible here. Key findings: elongation at break of the parent material strongly influences ductility of the printed tensegrity module; geometric/production defects significantly degrade mechanical response; allowing free deformation consistent with the infinitesimal mechanism is crucial; and post-critical behavior of struts was observed. Planned follow-ups include studying local strut stability, developing tensegrity models with rigid joints, testing other module types, and printing larger supercells/lattices. The excerpt does not provide data on multi-material rigid–flexible prints (e.g., PETG/TPU) or detailed impact-absorption metrics.

contexts.context: Pajunen et al. (2019) present a 3D-printable, single-material design that reproduces the mechanical response of pin-jointed tensegrity structures with elastically buckling struts. They base the unit cell on a truncated regular octahedron (a tessellatable geometry) and note the specific unit has 12 struts and 36 cables. Rather than using physical pin joints and separate tension members, the authors obtain an equivalent geometry via geometric manipulations to produce a manufacturable single-material part that requires no post-processing and is adaptable to different printers/materials. Numerical simulations (ABAQUS) guided quasi-static compression tests and dynamic drop-weight impact experiments. The printed tensegrity-inspired unit shows post-buckling stability, high elastic strain-energy absorption, resilience under severe deformation, and load-limiting behavior. The paper experimentally corroborates prior theoretical models of buckling tensegrity and proposes the cell as a promising building block for architected impact-absorbing metamaterials. The excerpt does not provide details on multi-material (rigid/soft like PETG/TPU) printing parameters, nor specific numerical impact-absorption metrics, which would need to be obtained from the full paper or complementary studies by Rimoli, Fraternali, and others.

snippets: We present the design of a 3D-printable structure with comparable response characteristics as a pin-jointed tensegrity structure.
The structure’s geometry maintains key tensegrity characteristics, thus generating an equivalent mechanical response.
Numerical simulations inform quasi-static compression experiments and dynamic drop weight impact tests.

The structure’s responses correspond well to the pin-jointed tensegrity, exhibiting desirable characteristics such as post-buckling stability, resilience under severe deformation, high elastic strain energy absorption, and load-limitation.
The tensegrity structure is shown in Fig. 1 (a). The structure has 12 struts and 36 cables.
This method uses a single material for the entire structure, has no post-processing, and can be adapted to a variety of printers and materials.
This work is the first to experimentally corroborate theoretical studies of buckling tensegrity structures.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes design and homogenization parameters for 3D-printable tensegrity metamaterials (cuboctahedron tessellation block). The authors use a linear elastic model with polymer-like properties representative of 3D printing: strut Young’s modulus E_S = 2600 MPa, cable Young’s modulus E_C = 12 MPa, and mass density ρ = 1.18×10^−3 g/mm^3. A cuboctahedron unit cell (13 struts, 96 cables) is modeled inside a 10 mm cubic box; members are circular with maximum strut radius r = 0.5 mm (A_S = 0.25π mm^2). Prestress is a design variable; an example prestress of σ11 = 0.60 MPa (0.05 E_C) is used to compute homogenized elasticity tensors for dense and porous tessellations. The homogenized elasticity tensor D is obtained via computational homogenization with periodic boundary conditions and presented in Voigt (6×6 symmetric) form. Topology and prestress provide rich design space: the block has 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms stabilized by prestress. The study assumes prestressed configurations remain within infinitesimal (linear) deformations. These parameters (unit cell size, member radii, material moduli, prestress levels, and homogenized D) are directly usable when comparing or designing 3D-printed tensegrity lattices, though the excerpt does not mention specific multi-material pairs like PETG/TPU nor the works of Pajunen, Rimoli, or Fraternali or explicit impact-absorption test results.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron topology used in NASA’s SUPERball work and the ReCTeR prototype. The basic tensegrity icosahedron configuration has 6 rigid struts and 24 outer spring-cable assemblies; a payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies to suspend a payload. ReCTeR is an untethered, underactuated 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron prototype (mass 1.1 kg). It uses 24 passive outer spring-cable assemblies with low-stiffness springs (28.4 N/m) pretensioned to ≈10 N, and six actuated spring-cable assemblies routed through the structure. Actuated cables change rest length via DC motors (4.5 W, 4.4:1 gear ratio) that spool on a 5.5 mm snag-resistant bobbin; the cable’s other end connects to a stiffer spring (81 N/m). Sensing includes 24 tension sensors (strain gages), six ground-reaction-force sensors, and three 6-DOF IMUs; batteries and comms are integrated into struts making it untethered. Two simulators are used: an Euler–Lagrange simulator (good for structural forces, stiffness, and impact/payload acceleration prediction but limited for rich environment interaction) and the NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT). NTRT is built on the discrete-time Bullet Physics engine and includes a custom library modeling spring-cable assemblies as two-point tensional elements applying directional forces; initially cables lacked physical collisions but an efficient soft-body contact dynamics capability was later implemented to allow realistic elastic-cable interactions with terrain. The excerpt does not provide explicit node counts, overall robot dimensions, or any details about the Berkeley ULTRA-Spine.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents design and performance details for NASA's SUPERball tensegrity prototype. SUPERball is a 6-strut tensegrity (icosahedron-derived) robot composed of hollow aluminum tubes with 12 autonomous end-cap units; it has 24 spring-cable assemblies but only 12 actuators (one actuator per two cables) using 100 W BLDC motors. Early design targets (from NTRT-informed simulations) specified 1.5 m struts, average cable tensions of ~75 N, peak tensions of ~200 N, and compressive strut loads up to ~800 N, with actuators able to change cable length at ~0.2 m/s. Tabled prototype values show a 2014 configuration: lstrut 1.5 m, ∆lact 0.2 m, kpassive 613 N/m, 12 actuators, mass ~9 kg; and a 2015 build: lstrut 1.7 m, ∆lact 0.42 m, kpassive 998 N/m, 12 actuators, mass ~21 kg (3.5 kg per strut including batteries). Sensors include force, length (encoders), motor torque, and IMU. The report notes packing/launch constraints (aeroshell diameter limits, example: 3.8 m struts to fit behind a 4.5 m aeroshell) and suggests deployable/telescoping struts as future work. contexts.context: The excerpt describes SUPERball as a 6-strut icosahedron tensegrity robot built from 6 structural rods that form an icosahedral shape when all cables are equal length. ReCTeR is an earlier prototype: it has 6 motors distributed across 3 rods and uses a combination of 24 main structural (passive) cables and 6 additional actuated interior cables to increase force for rolling. SUPERball increases embedded actuation: it has 12 motors (one per end-cap). Each SUPERball rod is made of two modular end-cap assemblies plus a connecting strut tube; each end-cap contains the mechanical and electrical systems, can be removed as a unit, and (in the reported design) is capable of closed-loop actuation of one cable. The modular end-cap design and cable mounting brackets allow different arrangements of actuated and passive cables, supporting heterogeneous tensegrity morphologies. The Dynamic Tensegrity Robotics Lab is developing the NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT), a simulated physics-based environment for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies; NTRT is being released as open-source. The excerpt does not provide explicit node counts, precise geometry dimensions, full cable count for the complete SUPERball (beyond analogy to 24 structural cables and actuated cables in ReCTeR), nor any information about the ULTRA-Spine project from Berkeley.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the NASA SUPERball tensegrity robot as an untethered, highly dynamic, compliant platform intended to combine entry/descent/landing (EDL) and rover locomotion. The vehicle uses spring-cable assemblies as tensile elements and has 24 spring-cable assemblies but only 12 onboard actuators, enabled by high-power (100 W) motors mounted in end caps. The actuator hookup uses a symmetric pattern of “actuated triangles,” with four of eight equilateral faces fully actuated; this actuator range allows motion primitives such as a punctuated roll that can be achieved with only one actuated cable (versus three for a prototyping kit). SUPERball is currently terrestrial but designed toward space constraints. For design and control, the Dynamic Tensegrity Robotics Lab developed and uses the NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT), an open-source simulator (URL given) to design/test robots, develop control strategies, study physical properties, and identify engineering requirements. The excerpt does not provide explicit counts of nodes, struts, total cables, precise dimensions, nor details about a 6-bar icosahedron topology or the ULTRA-Spine tensegrity spine robot from Berkeley.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Buckminster Fuller’s Ascension (Aspension) Dome concept as a cable-dome type formed by starting from a bicycle-wheel-like arrangement: radial cables link an outer compression ring to an inner tension ring, then the inner ring is duplicated with vertical bars and the process is repeated to create concentric layers (the model had eight layers). This Aspension Dome concept inspired large roof structures, notably David Geiger’s Olympic Fencing and Gymnastic Arena in Seoul (1988), a commonly cited example of a cable-dome (often called a Geiger dome). The text also discusses Kenneth Snelson’s tensegrity sculptures and towers: his X-piece influenced Fuller, and Snelson’s towers are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms (e.g., the 1968 Needle Tower I and the 1969 Needle Tower II). The excerpt does not discuss the Levy dome, the Georgia Dome, nor the deployable tensegrity masts by Tibert and Pellegrino, so information on those specific items is not available in these pages.

snippets: Another structural type devised by Buckminster Fuller was his A(scending su)spension Dome (Fig. 6), patented in 1964 [33]; its surprisingly simple, original concept may be deciphered with the help of Fig. 7.

On starting from the idealized bicycle wheel depicted in Fig. 7(a, b), where radial cables connect an outer compression ring to an inner tension ring, imagine duplicating the inner ring with the insertion of vertical bars, as shown in (c, d), and then continuing the process as suggested by (e, f) until a cable dome with the desired number of smaller and smaller concentric layers is obtained (the layers of the model Aspension Dome in Fig. 6 are eight).

The Aspension Dome was to serve as an inspiring model for a number of very large rooﬁng structures, beginning with the Olympic Fencing and Gymnastic Arena in Seoul (South Korea), realized by David Geiger in 1988 (Fig. 8).

When the latter, one of his resident students at the Black Mountain College in North Carolina, presented his X-piece to him [1], Buckminster Fuller was more struck by the innovative structural implications than by the three-dimensional visual impact of that sculpture.

Snelson’s towers are built by juxtaposition along a vertical axis of smaller and smaller tensegrity prisms; the 1968 20-meter Needle Tower I shown in Fig. 2b is located in Washington, D.C., the 1969 30-meter Needle Tower II in Otterlo (Holland).
Winds make Snelson’s towers sound as quite unusual musical instruments.

contexts.context: The excerpt analyzes the Georgia Dome as a tensegrity/cable-dome prototype and contrasts two cable-dome approaches: Geiger’s radial cable-and-strut (circular cable dome) and Levy’s triangulated network. Materials and sizing used in the analysis are given (φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires, tensile strength 1670 N/mm2; Q345 circular tube struts, yield 345 N/mm2) and a uniform roof load of 0.6 kN/m2 is applied. Member areas for ridge, diagonal, hoop cables and struts are listed. Nonlinear FE analysis showed largely linear force variation with load but different cable types respond differently (e.g., ridge cable forces decrease; hoop cable forces increase). The primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section rather than cable breakage or strut buckling. To increase capacity, the study recommends increasing prestress in inner/upper ridge and diagonal cables (strengthening the central section). Fu’s proposed structural type 1 combines cable-dome semicircles for simplicity with a triangulated, stiffer central rectangular section to resist horizontal displacement and improve bearing capacity.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses design and structural behavior of quasi-elliptical tensegrity/cable domes, using the Georgia Dome as a prototype and proposing two alternative structural types. It describes member sizing (e.g., ridge, diagonal and hoop cable cross-sections) and a Type 2 scheme where the central section is rigid bars connected by a transverse truss, effectively a cable dome split and joined by a central truss. A cost-weighting approach treats cable weight as twice that of steel to produce a nominal steel weight for cost comparison; Table 1 compares Georgia Dome and the two proposed types (Type 1 lower weight but less stiff; Type 2 heavier but stiffer with smaller vertical displacement). Key behavioral conclusions note that tensegrity domes differ from conventional domes: failure is often slackening of ridge/diagonal cables, and the central section is the weakest requiring strengthened horizontal stiffness. For long spans (~200 m) either wedge-shaped cable networks or triangulated networks (or a combination) are appropriate. The excerpt cites Geiger and Levy concerning cable domes (Korean Olympics, hypar-tensegrity, Georgia Dome), but it does not describe Snelson, Tibert or Pellegrino deployable masts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Geiger cable domes as assemblies of cable and strut elements—nested circular configurations with vertical struts connected to cable networks. Although this arrangement shares the cable–strut composition of tensegrity systems, conventional Geiger struts do not act to balance tension with compression as tensegrity struts do. The paper proposes a new cable-dome configuration that mimics tensegrity behaviour so applied loads are distributed across all elements rather than producing highly local effects. contexts.context: The excerpt explains tensegrity as an architectural principle — “tensional integrity” — in which tensile prestress provides mechanical stability. Cells are described as using tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: the cytoskeleton is the internal molecular framework that governs cell shape and mechanical stability. Cytoskeletal biopolymers continuously remodel, and some (notably contractile actomyosin filaments) actively generate tension via ATP-driven molecular motors. The authors emphasize hierarchical and multimodular tensegrity: smaller tensegrity modules can combine into larger systems, such that disruption of a single element in multimodular assemblies need not destabilize the whole. Importantly, tensegrity enables long-range force transmission and redistribution — force applied to one element is redistributed and can rearrange elements across scales — allowing mechanical signals to be channeled from macro- to nanoscale and facilitating mechanochemical conversion. Theoretical tensegrity models are presented as tools to predict cell behaviors and to place this view in context with other physical models of the cell.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains tensegrity as architectures composed of continuous tension elements and discontinuous compression elements, with two mathematical classes (prestressed and geodesic). Key mechanical features are prestress, triangulation, intrinsic self-stabilization, force transmission throughout the structure, and return to shape after loading; continuous tension with discontinuous compression yields efficient, lightweight, strong forms. Biotensegrity applies these principles across hierarchical biological levels (molecular to organ systems), with early applications focusing on the human spine and the idea that the spine does not act as a simple compressive column. Donald Ingber developed the cellular tensegrity concept: cells are prestressed structures (cytoskeleton + adhesions) that transmit external forces through the cell, change shape under release, and exert prestress onto the extracellular substrate (cells pulling on and wrinkling flexible substrates). The excerpt emphasizes force transfer, prestress, and hierarchical linkage of levels.
