Levin applies tensegrity thinking to the spine, cervical spine, shoulder girdle, and conceptualizes the scapula functionally ("The scapula is a sesamoid bone"), implying bone elements act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network. Ingber (with Jamieson and later with Wang & Butler) is cited for the cellular tensegrity concept: cells as prestressed, tensegrity structures where the cytoskeleton transmits forces across the cell surface and mediates mechanotransduction. Huijing’s work on myofascial force transmission is also referenced, supporting the idea of force transmission through continuous soft-tissue tension. Together these references indicate a multiscale tensegrity principle in biology: rigid/compressive elements (bones, cytoskeletal microtubules) embedded in a network of tensile elements (muscles, fascia, actin filaments, intermediate filaments) that maintain shape, distribute loads efficiently, enable adaptability, and permit mechanical signaling (mechanotransduction).

snippets: Tensegrity is a scale-free structural system that has evoked interest e.g. in architects, engineers, space engineers, scientists, and biologists (Hanaor 2012) as well as movement and manual therapy practitioners (Scarr 2011; Swanson II 2013; Hohenschurz-Schmidt, Esteves and Thomson 2016).

The word ´tensegrity´ is a combination of two words: tension (or tensile by Hanaor 2012) (or tensional by Swanson II 2013) and integrity that describe tensioned or pre-stressed structure and  its architecture that follows certain mathematical rules.

A technical definition where “tensegrity” stands for systems in a stable self-equilibrated state comprising a (discontinuous) set of compressed components and inside a continuum of tensioned components (Rhode-Barbarigos 2012).

Most manmade structures are stabilized by gravita-tional compression. In contrast, tensegrity systems are self-stabilized through force tri-angulation and would maintain their shape in the absence of gravity (Swanson II 2013).

The tensegrity model has the potential to elevate the traditional mechanistic model to meet the current deficiencies of its postulates (Ingber 2003a; Ingber 2003b; Swanson II 2013; Levin et al. 2017; Scarr 2020; Sharkey 2021).
Biotensegrity is the application of tensegrity principles to biological structures (Levin in Hutson and Ellis 2006; Swanson II 2013).
The model of tensegrity originates in arts and architecture and was formerly developed in the 1960’s.
The same fundamental mathematical rules describe the closest packing of spheres (Connelly and Back 1998; Ingber 2003; Levin in Hutson and Ellis 2006).

contexts.context: Bauer et al. present space-tileable tensegrity metamaterials built from a truncated-octahedron–based unit cell whose recursive reflection forms 2 × 2 × 2 supercells and larger space-filling arrays. The design intentionally creates isolated compressive-member loops that do not form continuous compressive paths through the 6 × 6 × 6-cell metamaterial. This compression-member discontinuity drives a mechanical response that suppresses localized failure: measured and simulated uniaxial compression tests show a compression discontinuity that prevents localized failure propagation and produces a homogeneous, delocalized deformation distribution. From a systems perspective, these tensegrity metamaterials avoid negative-stiffness events and display a stable, monotonic stress–strain response, enabling orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption and up to a reported 25-fold enhancement in deformability relative to same-strength state-of-the-art lattice architectures. The paper frames this delocalization strategy as a route to failure-resistant, lightweight load-bearing systems. (The provided excerpt does not describe manufacturing details such as 3D printing nor Ruffini et al.’s characterization; those items are not present in the excerpt.)

contexts.context: The excerpt (Pajunen et al., with Julian J. Rimoli among the authors) describes using a truncated-octahedron tensegrity as the baseline unit cell for tensegrity-inspired metamaterials. The unit cell has 12 struts and 36 cables and is suitable for tessellation in three-dimensional lattices. The authors design a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent of a pin-jointed tensegrity that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity and compressive response to tensegrities with elastically buckling struts. Buckling in struts produces a stress–strain plateau and substantially increases elastic strain-energy absorption; the printed design exhibits post-buckling stability, resilience under severe deformation, and load-limitation. Numerical ABAQUS simulations guided quasi-static compression experiments and dynamic drop-weight impact tests to characterize dynamic response and energy absorption. The fabrication approach emphasizes a single-material print with no post-processing and adaptability to different printers and materials. The paper reports this is the first experimental corroboration of theoretical studies on buckling tensegrity structures and positions the design as a promising manufacturable unit cell for architected metamaterials. The excerpt does not include characterizations by Bauer et al. or Ruffini et al.

contexts.context: The excerpt outlines core concepts relevant to deployable tensegrity masts and their simulation/design tools. Pellegrino (cited) frames deployable tensegrity systems as transformable structures whose stiffness and stability come from self-stress; therefore controlling the self-stress (via element-length variation and actuation) enables active deployment. Motro/Pellegrino recommend combining physical, geometrical and numerical models to identify required active elements, ideal geometric transformation paths, and the real (simulated) paths. Deployment is modeled as a nonlinear, path-constrained optimization with key constraints including structural integrity throughout motion, avoiding strut collisions, and maintaining cable tension to prevent entanglement. Cable-controlled deployment based on following an equilibrium manifold is noted as an advantageous strategy (Sultan & Skelton), keeping the structure near prestressable equilibria during transformation. Use of continuous cables introduces alternative actuation strategies (strut-routed, single cable-routed, multiple cable-routed) that reduce embedded actuators. The excerpt also notes that advanced computational/control techniques (case-based reasoning, reinforcement learning, stochastic search) have been applied to active tensegrity control and simulation at EPFL, which is pertinent when evaluating software like MOTES, topology tools, or simulators.

snippets: Tensegrity structures have several promising properties for transformable applications.
Since their stability and stiffness is provided by self-stress, appropriate control of  self-stress can lead to active and deployable systems (Pellegrino 2001).
The control of tensegrity systems requires element-length variations and therefore actuation.
Designing deployable tensegrity systems is a challenging task due to a large number of constraints (Sultan, Hassan et al. 2009).
Common constraints for the tensegrity-deployment problem are structural integrity, strut collision and cable-entanglement issues.
Motro et al. (Pellegrino 2001) proposed the use of physical, geometrical and numerical models for the design of deployable tensegrity systems.
An advantageous cable-controlled deployment scheme for tensegrity systems was proposed by Sultan and Skelton (2003).
The equilibrium manifold describes a continuous set of solutions of the prestressability problem (Sultan and Skelton 2003; Skelton and de Oliveira 2009; Sultan, Hassan et al. 2009).
Employing continuous cables in tensegrity systems results in novel actuation strategies (Moored, Kemp et al. 2011).
In strut-routed actuation, active continuous cables run along the struts.
Single cable-routed actuation employs a single continuous cable running over frictionless pulleys, while multiple cable-routed actuation employs multiple continuous cables

contexts.context: This paper investigates tensegrity-based cellular metamaterials and uses a continuum model (strain-energy equivalence with a discrete formulation) to identify their effective elasticity and extreme mechanical behavior. The authors focus on lattices constructed from supercells of simplex modules and state that "Three representative tensegrity lattices based on the 4-strut simplex module are discussed." Mechanical response can be tuned by changing member properties or the level of self-equilibrated (pre-)stress. The work includes nonlinearities from equilibrium in the actual (pre-stressed) configuration. Lattices are classified via eigenanalysis of the equivalent 6×6 elasticity matrix, allowing identification as extreme materials (very stiff for some stress states and very compliant for others). The paper defines six representative deformation modes: "stiff, soft and medium extensional modes and high (double) as well as low shear modes." The authors note tensegrities are pin-jointed cable–strut systems, statically indeterminate and stable, and observe lattices can be unimode or nearly bimode per the extreme-materials classification. contexts.context: The excerpt explains key characteristics of tensegrity and tensegrity-like unit cells relevant to additive manufacturing. Tensegrity units combine compression bars and tension-only cables; they can exhibit first-order infinitesimal mechanisms (soft-modes) defined by nodal displacements that induce only second-order member elongations, and they also admit selfstress states that preload members and alter stiffness. The triangular tensegrity prism (T3) is used as an example: it has one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent selfstress state, with the mechanism being a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases and the selfstress shown as axial forces at nodes. The authors discuss how tuning geometry and selfstress can produce stiffening or softening nonlinear responses, enable bistability/multistability, and permit tessellation into lattice metamaterials. The continuum model proposed in [20] and analysed in [21] is based on the equivalence of the strain energy of an unsupported tensegrity structure defined with the use of the finite element method (FEM) [23–26] and the strain energy of a solid determined using the symmetric linear 3D elasticity theory (LTE) [27].
The strain energy of a tensegrity truss according to FEM is dependent on the global linear stiffness matrix KL and the global geometric stiffness matrix KG = S0Kg.
The applied continuum model can be used for the analysis of both tensegrity unit cells and lattice structures or materials composed of these cells.
As the results obtained for single modules correspond to the properties of materials constructed from them, the conclusions can be drawn in regard to whole lattice metamaterials.
The number of eigenvalues that are close to zero indicates the type of extreme material, which can be: nullmode, unimode, bimode, trimode, quadramode, pentamode or hexamode [1,2].

snippets: The main focus of the present paper is put on the identiﬁcation of extreme mechanical properties of ﬁve regular tensegrity modules.
The considered structures are assumed to be used as unit cells in 3D lattice metamaterials.
The following tensegrity modules are analysed: 4-strut simplex, 3-strut simplex, expanded octahedron, truncated tetrahedron and X-module.
It is shown that the material, in which all modules are arranged in accordance with their inﬁnitesimal mechanisms, has the same mechanical properties as its unit cell
Extreme features of the proposed metamaterials are identiﬁed with the use of the continuum model, which enables the authors to ﬁnd the equivalent elasticity matrices of the examined structures.
Analysis of these matrices leads to the determination of eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors which, on the other hand, enable the identiﬁcation of soft and stiff deformation modes.

For each analysed module and thus for the metamaterial based on this module, a line of extreme mechanical properties is determined. It is a line on the plane k, σ, on which the smallest eigenvalue of the elasticity matrix is close to zero and which deﬁnes the possibility of the soft mode of deformation.
They have one stiff, one purely soft, some quasi-soft and some medium deformation modes.
The truncated tetrahedron module shows the most extreme properties, as it has three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes.
The expanded octahedron has three stiff, one purely soft and two quasi-soft modes of deformation and moreover, the biggest area of positive deﬁniteness of the elastic matrix.

The X-module has one stiff and one soft mode and the smallest area for which the elastic matrix is positive deﬁnite, but in the same time, it is quite simple to create, it has small amount of elements and may be formed in very regular patterns.

A metamaterial based on the 4-strut simplex module is identiﬁed as quasi bimode, 3-strut simplex and expanded octahedron as a quasi trimode, truncated tetrahedron as a trimode and X-module as a unimode.

the truncated tetrahedron module cannot be considered as a potential unit cell of the metamaterial, because the parameters k and σ, for which the soft mode is obtained are not achievable with the current technology.

contexts.context: The excerpt outlines general properties of tensegrity lattice metamaterials relevant to unit-cell design and additive manufacturing. Tensegrity frameworks are prestressed, pin-connected lattices of bars and cables that typically include internal mechanisms and can exhibit multistability (bistability) by varying element lengths or self-stress. Examples illustrated include triangular tensegrity prisms and expanded octahedron (tensegrity icosahedron) geometries. A key fabrication challenge is the differing nature of bars versus thin tensile cables; a common practical approach is to realize tensegrity connectivity using only struts (thicker bars) which introduces bending that can be mitigated by tapering strut ends or using flexible hinges. The paper uses multiphoton lithography (MPL) to fabricate bistable tensegrity-like lattices with nanoscale features (minimum strut radii ~250 nm). Experimentally, assemblies show a softening equilibrium branch from the primary stable state, followed by a snapping event to a secondary stable state; the transition involves a preserved twisting mechanism and repeats under loading-unloading cycles. The excerpt does not provide specific details about the 4-strut simplex or truncated-tetrahedron modules by Sabouni-Zawadzka nor a formal classification of all soft vs stiff deformation modes, beyond mentioning internal mechanisms, twisting transitions, and softening/snapping behavior.

snippets: An intriguing category of lattice metamaterials is that of tensegrity frameworks: prestressed pin-connected lattices composed of bars (i.e., members loaded in compression) and cables (members loaded in tension), which typically feature internal mechanisms.
Some tensegrity modules can transcend from one stable state to two other stable states, either by changing the lengths of their elements or by changing the selfstress level
One of the main obstacles to the fabrication of tensegrity metamaterials is ensconced in the different nature of their constituent elements.
Fabricating lattice structures with the same nodal positions and connectivity of a tensegrity structure, but equipped with only thick (or moderately thick) struts, surmounts this fabrication barrier.
Bending can be mitigated by tapering the struts at the ends, or by using flexible hinges

MPL is a convenient fabrication technique with which to manufacture the structures examined in the present study, with the desired resolution, since they involve cylindrical struts with minimum features (cross-section radii) of 250 nm.

The force-displacement curves exhibited by the examined structures show a softening type response along the equilibrium branch initiating from the primary stable configuration. Such a branch terminates with a snapping event that drives the system into the secondary stable configuration.
The twisting mechanism that characterizes such a transition is preserved after unloading and during repeated loading-unloading cycles.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses the distinction between classic rigid/flexed/hinged structural solutions and tension-based systems, noting tension (cables, membranes) are abundant in space technology for preloading and shape control. It defines tensegrity as systems where solid compression-bearing elements are not directly connected but are held by a network of tension elements (struts suspended in cables). It states tensegrity has been used for space applications—typically columns or rings supporting instruments or holding reflector rims—and cites several US patents as examples (US 3,063,521; US 3,913,109; US 4,380,013; US 5,635,946; US 5,909,197). It also calls out specific disclosures: US 6,050,526 (deployable structure suspending a reflective film between flexible rods coupled to a solar panel) and US 7,806,370 B2 (use of cable diagonals for stiffening). The text emphasizes that prior tensegrity proposals generally treat rigid elements as structural and notes that proposals relying on weak natural force fields (photonic pressure, gravity gradient) lack the preloading needed for precision. The excerpt does not mention a Stern and Knight deployable tensegrity antenna nor any Daraio patents for wave generation, so those items are not covered here.

In the context of space, tensegrity structures typically take the form of tensegrity columns or rings in which tension and tension-compression elements (e.g., cables and rods) together form the column or the ring, to support some instrument at the end or to hold the rim of a flexible reflector surface (e.g., the dish surface of a mesh antenna) within.

contexts.context: The excerpt is U.S. Patent US 6,441,801 B1 (issued Aug. 27, 2002) titled for a deployable antenna using screw-motion control of a tensegrity support architecture. Inventors listed include Byron F. Knight, Joseph Duffy, Carl David Crane III and Joseph Rooney; the assignee is Harris Corporation. The disclosed structure is a screw motion-driven tensegrity antenna support that stably deploys and adjustably controls an energy-focusing surface (e.g., an RF wave-reflecting mesh). The mechanical layout is a parallel-platform tensegrity consisting of an upper hexagonal platform and a lower hexagonal base whose perimeters are formed by tensioned ties. Corresponding vertices are joined by leg pairs composed of a compression strut and a tension tie; structural stability requires that the sum of tie tensions match compression forces in the struts. Deployment and geometry control are achieved by a screw motion-based drive coupled to the struts to set relative rotation and pitch between upper platform and lower base. Question: Provide an in-depth, citation-rich literature survey of tensegrity structure designs (both canonical and non-canonical) that have been described in the academic, patent, and grey literature. Include, at minimum:
(1) Canonical Snelson-class prismatic tensegrities (T-bar / T-prism / n-bar prisms, with the stable twist angle theta = pi/2 - pi/n), including T3 (3-bar), T4 (4-bar), T6, and stacked/columnar prisms; (2) Polyhedral / spherical tensegrities -- 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, the SUPERball-class geometry), expanded octahedron, truncated tetrahedron, truncated octahedron, dodecahedral / rhombic tensegrities, and higher-genus spherical tensegrities by Pugh, Burkhardt, Skelton, Connelly & Whiteley, and Tibert & Pellegrino; (3) Class-k tensegrities (k>=2) where k struts share a node, including Skelton's class-2 columns and class-3 plates, T-bar / D-bar / Y-bar units, and Bendsoe-Skelton optimal mass tensegrities; (4) Tensegrity beams, columns, plates, and cylindrical / cylindrical deployable tensegrity masts (Snelson 'Needle Tower', Pellegrino, Skelton & Nagase, Sultan & Skelton, Bel Hadj Ali, Smaili & Motro 'tensegrity ring'); (5) Tensegrity domes, cable-domes, and Geiger / Levy / Fuller geodesic-derived tensegrities, including the Seoul Olympic Gymnastics Hall and Georgia Dome cable-domes; (6) Bio-inspired and morphologically-novel tensegrities -- Levin's biotensegrity (spinal column, knee, shoulder, cytoskeleton), tensegrity robots (NASA SUPERball v1/v2, Berkeley ULTRA-Spine, Tensegrity Spine, T-bar quadrupeds, TenseBot, Spherobot, Mori & Hirose helical tensegrity, EVA series, snake/worm tensegrity robots), tensegrity wings/UAVs, tensegrity grippers, soft-tensegrity manipulators, MEMS / micro-tensegrities, origami- and kirigami-tensegrity hybrids, knitted / woven tensegrity textiles, and lattice/metamaterial tensegrities; # Comprehensive Literature Survey of Tensegrity Structure Designs

## 1. Introduction

Tensegrity ("tensional integrity") structures comprise isolated compression members (struts/bars) suspended within a continuous network of tension members (cables/tendons), achieving self-equilibrium through internal prestress. Since Kenneth Snelson's 1948 X-piece sculpture and R. Buckminster Fuller's coinage of the term, tensegrity has evolved from art into a rich engineering paradigm spanning architecture, robotics, metamaterials, biology, and space exploration (malai2024tensegritystructurethe pages 41-47, micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). This survey systematically catalogs the major tensegrity design families described in the academic, patent, and grey literature, and concludes with specific recommendations for a BYU multi-material 3D-printing project.

---

## 2. Canonical Snelson-Class Prismatic Tensegrities

### 2.1 Three-Bar Prism (T3 / Simplex)
The simplest true tensegrity is the 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3): 3 struts, 9 cables (minimal) or 12 cables (non-minimal), and 6 nodes. Two triangular end-polygons are connected by struts with a characteristic stable twist angle θ = π/2 − π/n; for n = 3, θ = 30° (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2, oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40). The T3 possesses one independent infinitesimal mechanism and one independent self-stress state; the mechanism is a combined vertical translation and rotation of the bases, stabilized by the self-stress (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4). Oliveira and Skelton present this as the foundational "regular minimal tensegrity prism," noting that non-minimal variants with 12 strings provide higher stiffness and eliminate soft modes (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40).

### 2.2 Four-Bar Prism (T4 / 4-Strut Simplex)
The 4-strut simplex consists of 4 struts and 12 cables arranged in an 8-node prism with one base rotated 135° relative to the other. Sabouni-Zawadzka and Gilewski classify it as a "quasi-bimode" extreme metamaterial unit cell, featuring stiff, soft, and medium extensional modes plus high and low shear modes. The self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio serve as primary tuning parameters (sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 3-4, sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 1-3).

### 2.3 Higher-Order Prisms and Stacked Columns
The n-bar prism family generalizes to T6 (θ = 60°) and beyond. Prism twist angles cluster near 30–36° with cable pretension in the 1.8–2.5% engineering strain range for typical designs (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2). Snelson's iconic Needle Tower I (1968) and Needle Tower II (1969) are composed by stacking smaller tensegrity prisms to form columnar masts (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). Yildiz and Lesieutre developed effective continuum beam stiffness properties for n-strut cylindrical tensegrity towers, enabling homogenized analysis of long stacked-prism columns for space applications.

---

## 3. Polyhedral / Spherical Tensegrities

### 3.1 Six-Strut Tensegrity Icosahedron
The 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (also called Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron) is the canonical spherical tensegrity: 6 struts and 24 cables. This topology forms the basis of the NASA SUPERball robot, where the 2015 prototype featured 1.7 m struts, ~21 kg mass, 24 spring-cable assemblies, and 12 BLDC actuators (sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 1-2, sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 80-83). A payload variant adds 12 inner spring-cable assemblies for payload suspension (sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 29-32).

### 3.2 Expanded Octahedron
The expanded octahedron tensegrity has been studied as a metamaterial unit cell exhibiting three stiff modes, one purely soft mode, and two quasi-soft modes, with the largest positive-definite elasticity region among five compared regular tensegrity modules (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17). Vangelatos et al. fabricated expanded-octahedron-based bistable lattices using multiphoton lithography at nanoscale (minimum strut radii ~250 nm), demonstrating preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (vangelatos2020designandtesting pages 1-3).

### 3.3 Truncated Tetrahedron
The truncated tetrahedron module is identified as the most "extreme" regular tensegrity unit cell, featuring three purely stiff and three purely soft deformation modes (classified as a "trimode" material). However, its required self-stress and stiffness ranges lie beyond current practical fabrication limits (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 1-3).

### 3.4 Truncated Octahedron (Rimoli Cell)
The truncated octahedron tensegrity cell, introduced by Rimoli and Pal, has 12 struts and 36 cables and is inherently space-tileable. This cell is the foundation of the most important recent work on tensegrity metamaterials. Bauer et al. demonstrated that recursive reflection of truncated-octahedron cells into 2×2×2 and larger supercells creates metamaterials with isolated compression-member loops, suppressing localized failure and achieving up to 25-fold enhancement in deformability and orders-of-magnitude increases in energy absorption relative to same-strength conventional lattice architectures (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Pajunen et al. developed a 3D-printable, single-material equivalent that reproduces comparable strain-energy capacity with post-buckling stability and load-limiting behavior, validated through both quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact experiments (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2).

---

## 4. Class-k Tensegrities

Skelton defines a "class-k" tensegrity as one in which at most k rigid bodies share a node. Class-1 tensegrities have no strut-to-strut connections (the canonical definition), while higher classes permit shared nodes (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62, oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 98-111).

### 4.1 T-Bar and D-Bar Units
The **T-bar** unit replaces a single compression bar of length ℓ₀ with an internally tensegritized subassembly: in the cited example, 4 bars and 16 strings forming a class-4 tensegrity. Mass reduction occurs when the internal angle α₁ < 45° (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62). The **D-bar** is the dual of the T-bar, obtained by exchanging bars and strings; it is a class-2 tensegrity with string-to-string connections (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62). These building blocks enable Skelton's minimum-mass optimization framework.

### 4.2 Minimum-Mass Columns and Plates
Skelton and de Oliveira derive closed-form optimal mass expressions for class-2 tensegrity cylinders parameterized by radius R, half-bay height z, helix angle φ, and complexity q. The normalized mass J = Js + Jb is minimized under material yield constraints, with optimal complexity q* balancing structural efficiency against joint mass penalties (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 98-111). For any given aspect ratio ρ and complexity q, the optimal bending angle satisfies tan β* = ρ^(1/q), with asymptotic minimal cost J*∞ = 2 ln ρ⁻¹ as q → ∞ (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 47-62).

---

## 5. Tensegrity Domes and Cable-Domes

### 5.1 Geiger Cable-Dome (Seoul Olympic Halls)
David Geiger adapted Fuller's Aspension Dome concept into radial cable-and-strut domes for the Seoul Olympic Gymnastic and Fencing Arenas (1986/1988). These are technically "cable-domes" rather than pure tensegrities because the outer compression ring is not embedded within the cable network (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 1-4, micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). Micheletti and Podio-Guidugli trace the lineage from Fuller's bicycle-wheel-like arrangement through Geiger's implementation (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6).

### 5.2 Levy Cable-Dome (Georgia Dome)
Levy revised Geiger's radial layout with a triangulated cable network for the Georgia Dome (1992). Fu's nonlinear FE analysis showed that the primary failure mode is slackening of ridge and diagonal cables in the central section, with recommendations to increase prestress in inner cables for enhanced capacity (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 4-9, fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 9-13). The Georgia Dome used φ5 mm high-strength tensile wires (1670 N/mm²) and Q345 circular tube struts (345 N/mm²) under 0.6 kN/m² uniform roof load (fu2005structuralbehaviorand pages 4-9).

---

## 6. Bio-Inspired and Morphologically Novel Tensegrities

### 6.1 Biotensegrity (Levin, Ingber)
Levin's biotensegrity framework models musculoskeletal structures—spine, shoulder, pelvis—as "continuous tension, discontinuous compression" systems where bones act as compressive struts within a tensioned soft-tissue network (levin2007chapter15– pages 9-9, scarr2020biotensegritywhatis pages 1-2). Ingber's cellular tensegrity model demonstrates that cells use tensegrity architecture at the molecular level: actin-myosin filaments generate contractile tension (prestress), microtubules serve as compression struts, and intermediate filaments act as guy wires (swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 4-6, ingber2008tensegritybasedmechanosensingfrom pages 5-7, ingber2008tensegritybasedmechanosensingfrom pages 9-10, ingber2014tensegritycellularbiophysics pages 1-3). This hierarchical principle operates across scales from single proteins to whole organisms, with mechanotransduction enabled by long-range force transmission through the tensegrity network (swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 6-8, swanson2013biotensegrityaunifying pages 2-4).

### 6.2 Tensegrity Robots
**NASA SUPERball v1/v2**: A 6-strut icosahedron robot for planetary exploration, featuring 24 spring-cable assemblies and 12 actuators. The v1 (2015) measured ~1.7 m diameter, ~21 kg, with passive cable stiffness ~998 N/m and nominal actuated tension ~250 N (sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 1-2, sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 80-83). SUPERball v2 was redesigned to survive impact velocities upward of 8 m/s with 24 actuators and compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch). The **NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit (NTRT)** is an open-source simulator built on the Bullet Physics engine, released for rapid exploration of tensegrity morphologies and control strategies (sabelhaus2014hardwaredesignand pages 1-2, sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 2-3).

**Berkeley ULTRA-Spine**: A flexible actuated spine robot using stacked tensegrity vertebra modules, controlled via model-predictive control with inverse statics optimization (sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 29-32). The TT-3 robot from UC Berkeley is a modular, rod-centered 6-bar tensegrity with distributed actuation and control architecture.

---

## 7. Tensegrity Space Structures and Deployable Systems

### 7.1 Deployable Tensegrity Masts
Tibert and Pellegrino developed deployable tensegrity mast concepts using stacked Snelson-type prisms, investigating both strut-mode deployment for eight-stage masts and tendon-controlled strategies (micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 21-23). Sultan and Skelton proposed cable-controlled deployment following equilibrium manifolds to maintain structural integrity throughout transformation (rhodebarbarigos2012anactivedeployable pages 34-37).

### 7.2 Deployable Antenna Patents
**US 6,441,801 B1** (Knight et al., 2002): A screw-motion-driven tensegrity antenna with a parallel-platform architecture consisting of upper hexagonal platform and lower hexagonal base connected by compression strut and tension tie leg pairs (US6441801B1 pages 2-9, US6441801B1 pages 9-10, US6441801B1 pages 1-2). **US 6,542,132 B2** (Stern, 2003): A deployable reflector antenna with tensegrity support architecture and mounting frame for improved specific mass and compact stowage (US6542132B2 pages 1-9, US6542132B2 pages 9-10).

### 7.3 Wave Generation Patent
**US 8,616,328 B2** (Daraio, 2013): A tensegrity apparatus composed of multiple tensegrity units for transmitting solitary waves with adjustable profiles into materials or structures, enabling nondestructive evaluation applications (US8616328B2 pages 1-2).

## 8. Tensegrity-Inspired Metamaterials and Additive Manufacturing

### 8.1 Truncated Octahedron Lattices (Rimoli, Pajunen, Bauer)
The truncated-octahedron tensegrity cell (12 struts, 36 cables) is the leading architecture for 3D-printable impact-absorbing metamaterials. Pajunen et al. developed a single-material 3D-printable equivalent validated through ABAQUS simulations, quasi-static compression, and drop-weight impact tests (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2). Bauer et al. achieved unprecedented failure resistance with up to 25-fold deformability enhancement and orders-of-magnitude increased energy absorption through delocalized deformation enabled by compression-member discontinuity (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Ruffini and Rimoli used graph theory to show that deformation delocalization correlates with asymmetric tension-compression connectivity, providing design principles for failure-resistant metamaterials.

### 8.2 Tunable Tensegrity Tessellations
Liu et al. developed a cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation block (13 struts, 96 cables) with 12 independent prestress states and 17 internal mechanisms, using polymer-like material properties (E_S = 2600 MPa, E_C = 12 MPa) representative of multi-material 3D printing. Computational homogenization demonstrated rich tunability of effective stiffness and bandgaps (liu2019unravelingtensegritytessellations pages 7-9).

### 8.3 Bistable Tensegrity Units
Intrigila et al. fabricated bistable double-triangular-prism units via stereolithography, demonstrating snap-through behavior with preserved twisting mechanisms under cyclic loading (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 12-12). Vangelatos et al. extended this to nanoscale using multiphoton lithography with 250 nm minimum feature sizes (vangelatos2020designandtesting pages 1-3).

### 8.4 Simplex-Based Lattice Metamaterials
Sabouni-Zawadzka systematically compared five regular tensegrity unit cells—4-strut simplex (quasi-bimode), 3-strut simplex (quasi-trimode), expanded octahedron (quasi-trimode), truncated tetrahedron (trimode), and X-module (unimode)—identifying soft and stiff deformation modes via eigenanalysis of equivalent elasticity matrices (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 1-3). Self-stress level and cable-to-strut stiffness ratio are the primary tuning parameters, with six representative deformation modes: stiff, soft, and medium extensional, plus high (double) and low shear (sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 1-3).

## 9. Topology Generation and Computational Design Methods

### 9.1 Form-Finding Methods
Tibert and Pellegrino's 2003 review established the standard taxonomy of form-finding approaches: force-density methods, energy minimization, dynamic relaxation, and analytical solutions for regular topologies (uzun2017formfindingandanalysis pages 1-2). Recent advances include genetic-algorithm-based total potential energy minimization for free-form tensegrities (Uzun 2017) and deep neural networks for form-finding that substitute trained DNNs for eigenvalue decomposition of force-density matrices (Lee et al. 2022). Graph neural networks have also been applied to tensegrity form-finding (Shao et al. 2024).

### 9.2 Open-Source Software
Key open-source tools include: **NTRT (NASA Tensegrity Robotics Toolkit)**, built on the Bullet Physics engine for tensegrity robot simulation (sabelhaus2014hardwaredesignand pages 1-2, sabelhaus2015systemdesignand pages 2-3); **MOTES (MOdeling TENsegrity Structures)**, a MATLAB-based open-source tool by Skelton's group for statics, dynamics, and form-finding of general tensegrity systems; and various research codes for computational homogenization of tensegrity metamaterials.

### 9.3 Elastic Lattice Patent for Tensegrity Robots
**US 2019/0382995 A1** (Chen, 2019): An elastic lattice platform for rapid prototyping of tensegrity structures and robots, where tensile members form a spatially defined structure without compressive members touching.

### Key Rationale and Parameter Recommendations

**Top Priority: Truncated Octahedron Cell (Rank 1).** This cell has the strongest experimental validation for impact absorption (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). Its 12-strut/36-cable topology maps naturally to PETG compression members and TPU tension members. The Bambu H2D's multi-material capability can print PETG struts with TPU tendons in a single build, potentially eliminating post-assembly. Critical design variables for Bayesian optimization include: unit-cell edge length (5–20 mm), strut diameter (0.8–3 mm), TPU tendon diameter (0.4–1.5 mm), initial tendon prestrain (0–10%), node fillet radius, and lattice relative density (5–30%).

**Calibration Benchmark: T3 Simplex (Rank 2).** The 3-bar prism (3 struts, 9 cables, 6 nodes) is the ideal calibration geometry because it has a single self-stress state and single mechanism, enabling clean validation of PETG/TPU constitutive models and the prestress-printing workflow before scaling to more complex cells (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4).

**Stacked Prismatic Column (Rank 7).** Particularly suited to the crutch-tip application because its axial geometry matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios. Progressive bay collapse/twisting under axial impact can absorb energy through multiple stages, and functionally graded stiffness along the column height can be achieved by varying bay parameters.

**Material-Specific Parameters for Bayesian Optimization:**
- **PETG struts**: diameter (0.8–4 mm), wall thickness if hollow (0.4–1.2 mm), length/slenderness ratio (critical for Euler buckling plateau)
- **TPU tendons**: durometer (80A–95A), cross-section (0.4–2 mm diameter), initial stretch/prestrain (0–15%)
- **Interface**: node geometry/fillet radius, PETG-TPU bonding area, overhang angle constraints
- **Lattice-level**: cell count per axis (2×2×2 to 6×6×6), grading function, boundary/skin conditions, overall relative density

**Open-Source Resources:** The NASA NTRT simulator (open-source, GitHub) provides validated physics for tensegrity dynamics. MOTES (MATLAB open-source by Skelton's group) handles statics and form-finding. For CAD generation, the parametric geometry of all recommended cells can be scripted in Python/OpenSCAD from published node coordinates. The Pajunen/Rimoli truncated-octahedron cell geometry is fully specified in the literature and reproducible for STL generation (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, liu2019unravelingtensegritytessellations pages 7-9).

## 11. Conclusion

This survey documents the remarkable breadth of tensegrity structural designs spanning seven decades—from Snelson's original prismatic sculptures through NASA's SUPERball planetary lander to Rimoli's failure-resistant metamaterials. For the BYU multi-material 3D-printing project, the truncated-octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell emerges as the highest-priority starting geometry due to its validated impact performance, space-tileability, and natural compatibility with PETG-strut/TPU-tendon multi-material fabrication (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2). The 3-bar simplex provides the ideal calibration benchmark (oliveira2009tensegritysystems pages 15-40, intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4), while the 4-strut simplex and expanded octahedron offer rich intermediate complexity for parametric exploration (sabounizawadzka2020extrememechanicalproperties pages 15-17, sabounizawadzka2019softandstiff pages 3-4). Bistable double-prism units add snap-through energy absorption capabilities particularly suited to crutch-tip applications (intrigila2022fabricationandexperimental pages 4-4). The stacked prismatic column geometry most naturally matches the axial loading profile of a crutch tip (shaikh2026dynamicanalysisand pages 1-2, micheletti2022seventyyearsof pages 3-6). All recommended geometries have sufficient published geometric specifications for parametric CAD generation, and the rich design variable space—spanning strut/tendon dimensions, prestrain, cell count, grading, and material selection—is well-suited to Bayesian optimization for systematic performance improvement.

| Rank | Design Name | Topology (struts/cables) | Rationale for BYU Project | Key Design Variables for Bayesian Optimization | Printability Assessment (PETG/TPU multi-material) | Open-Source Resources Available | Primary Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Truncated octahedron tensegrity-inspired cell | 12 struts / 36 cables | Best starting point for energy-absorbing lattices: space-tileable, already validated in quasi-static compression and drop-weight impact, with post-buckling stability, load limiting, and high elastic energy absorption; also tied to delocalized-deformation metamaterial literature (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) | unit-cell edge length; strut diameter and wall thickness; tendon diameter; tendon modulus/infill; initial tendon prestrain; node fillet radius; strut taper; lattice relative density; cells across thickness; grading through depth | Excellent: naturally maps to PETG struts + TPU tendons; can be printed either as assembled multimaterial cell or as monolithic node-strut body with overprinted TPU tendons; best match to Bambu H2D workflow | CAD/mesh likely reproducible from literature; many printable tensegrity-inspired lattices are readily recreated; no canonical public URDF needed for static tests | Pajunen et al. 2019 (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000030) |
| 2 | 3-bar prismatic simplex (T3) | 3 struts / 9 cables | Simplest true tensegrity benchmark; minimal part count, well-understood self-stress/mechanism pair, ideal for calibrating PETG/TPU material models and validating prestress-printing methods before moving to larger lattices (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036) | prism height; base radius; twist angle; strut diameter; tendon diameter; initial TPU stretch/prestrain; node compliance; end-cap geometry; contact pad orientation for crutch-tip loading | Excellent: lowest assembly and failure complexity; easiest design for coupon-scale DOE and Bayesian optimization | Widely available maker CAD/STL variants online; strong academic reproducibility | Oliveira & Skelton 2009; Intrigila et al. 2022 (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000036) |
| 3 | 4-strut simplex | 4 struts / 12 cables | Strong candidate for tunable lattice mechanics: quasi-bimode behavior, regular rectangular packing advantages, and richer anisotropy than T3 while remaining printable and compact (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040) | base rotation angle; cell aspect ratio; strut diameter; tendon diameter; prestrain; cable/strut stiffness ratio; lattice orientation; supercell arrangement; graded density | Excellent: still low complexity, but gives more modes than T3; very suitable for PETG/TPU parametric sweeps | Can be rebuilt from literature geometry; likely easiest “metamaterial-ready” true tensegrity cell after T3 | Sabouni-Zawadzka & Gilewski 2019 (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000040) |
| 4 | Expanded octahedron | ~6 struts / not stated in retrieved context | Attractive middle ground between simple prisms and dense polyhedral cells; reported to have three stiff, one soft, and two quasi-soft modes plus a large positive-definite design region, suggesting broad tunability and robustness for impact-mitigation lattices (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000041) | cell size; octahedral expansion ratio; strut diameter; tendon diameter; prestress; strut slenderness; lattice orientation; stacking pattern | Very good: geometry is more complex than simplex cells but still feasible with PETG/TPU multimaterial printing | Literature-based reconstruction straightforward; no major robotics dependencies | Sabouni-Zawadzka 2020; Vangelatos et al. 2020 (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000041) |
| 5 | Bistable double prism | double T3-derived prism / compliant tension network | Especially promising for crutch tips because bistability and snap-through can create plateau-like force response and multi-stage energy absorption; useful if the goal expands from cushioning to reusable shock isolation (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000005) | primary/secondary stable-state geometry; hinge thickness; prism height; twist angle; tendon prestrain; compliant-joint thickness; trigger force; damping via TPU geometry | Very good: compliant multimaterial printing can realize hinges and tendons without post-assembly; ideal for prototyping nonlinear response | Literature geometry reproducible; good candidate for in-house CAD generation | Intrigila et al. 2022 (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000005) |
| 6 | Cuboctahedron tensegrity tessellation | 13 struts / 96 cables | Best if the project emphasizes wave filtering, stiffness tuning, or graded architected media rather than only crushing; rich design space with 12 prestress states and 17 mechanisms makes it ideal for surrogate-model-driven exploration (pqac-00000006) | box size; strut radius; tendon radius; prestress state selection; porous vs dense tessellation; periodicity; gradient across lattice; orientation; skin thickness if embedded in a crutch-tip shell | Moderate: high cable count increases print/assembly complexity, but multimaterial printing can eliminate manual lacing | Research code/CAD not confirmed, but geometry is well specified in literature | Liu et al. 2019 (pqac-00000006) |
| 7 | Stacked prismatic column | repeated T3 or n-bar prism bays / repeated cable sets | Strong candidate for crutch-tip inserts because axial impact can be absorbed through progressive bay collapse/twisting; column stacking also matches real crutch-tip aspect ratios and enables functionally graded stiffness along height (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018) | number of bays; bay height; inter-bay rotation; twist angle per bay; strut diameter; tendon prestrain; grading by bay; end-constraint stiffness; shell confinement | Very good: repeated modules are easy to scale and tune; excellent for print-test-learn loops | Easy to build from canonical prism CAD; abundant maker examples | Shaikh & Magar 2026; Snelson tower lineage (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000018) |
| 8 | T-bar unit / T-bar lattice | 4 bars / 16 strings in cited example | Interesting for negative-Poisson-like or lateral-compliance concepts and for replacing single compression members with internally tensegritized members; good secondary candidate after simpler cells are validated (pqac-00000031) | replacement-bar length; internal angle alpha; sub-bar diameter; tendon diameter; prestrain; unit orientation inside lattice; node block size | Moderate: more node complexity than simplex cells, but feasible with PETG nodes/struts and TPU tendons | Literature equations support direct CAD parameterization; public hobby files may exist but are less standardized | Oliveira & Skelton 2009 (pqac-00000031) |
| 9 | 6-bar icosahedron / SUPERball-class cell | 6 struts / 24 cables | Highly robust and impact-tolerant topology with obvious relevance to landers and crumple-resistant shells, but less space-efficient for dense lattices and overkill for first-generation crutch-tip studies; better for outer-shell or hybrid absorber concepts (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) | sphere diameter; strut length; tendon diameter; prestress; contact-face distribution; shell embedding; active vs passive cable subsets; lattice packing fraction | Moderate: very printable as a single demonstrator, but inefficient as a dense repeated lattice | Strong open-source ecosystem via NTRT/SUPERball models and maker builds | SunSpiral et al. 2015; Sabelhaus et al. 2015 (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| 10 | D-bar metamaterial / D-bar-derived cell | not stated in retrieved context | Worth exploring as a higher-risk, higher-novelty branch because class-2 dual topologies may unlock unusual deformation paths and potentially auxetic or anisotropic crushing behavior, but geometric complexity and sparse validation make it a later-stage candidate (pqac-00000031) | dual-cell proportions; tendon routing; node connectivity; prestrain; lattice orientation; confinement; mixed cell packing with T-bar or simplex units | Fair to moderate: printable, but topology definition and parameterization are less mature for rapid screening | Mostly literature-derived; likely requires custom CAD generation | Oliveira & Skelton 2009 (pqac-00000031) |

info.query:
Provide an in-depth, citation-rich literature survey of tensegrity structure designs (both canonical and non-canonical) that have been described in the academic, patent, and grey literature. Include, at minimum:
(1) Canonical Snelson-class prismatic tensegrities (T-bar / T-prism / n-bar prisms, with the stable twist angle theta = pi/2 - pi/n), including T3 (3-bar), T4 (4-bar), T6, and stacked/columnar prisms; (2) Polyhedral / spherical tensegrities -- 6-strut tensegrity icosahedron (Jessen's orthogonal icosahedron, the SUPERball-class geometry), expanded octahedron, truncated tetrahedron, truncated octahedron, dodecahedral / rhombic tensegrities, and higher-genus spherical tensegrities by Pugh, Burkhardt, Skelton, Connelly & Whiteley, and Tibert & Pellegrino; (3) Class-k tensegrities (k>=2) where k struts share a node, including Skelton's class-2 columns and class-3 plates, T-bar / D-bar / Y-bar units, and Bendsoe-Skelton optimal mass tensegrities; (4) Tensegrity beams, columns, plates, and cylindrical / cylindrical deployable tensegrity masts (Snelson 'Needle Tower', Pellegrino, Skelton & Nagase, Sultan & Skelton, Bel Hadj Ali, Smaili & Motro 'tensegrity ring'); (5) Tensegrity domes, cable-domes, and Geiger / Levy / Fuller geodesic-derived tensegrities, including the Seoul Olympic Gymnastics Hall and Georgia Dome cable-domes; (6) Bio-inspired and morphologically-novel tensegrities -- Levin's biotensegrity (spinal column, knee, shoulder, cytoskeleton), tensegrity robots (NASA SUPERball v1/v2, Berkeley ULTRA-Spine, Tensegrity Spine, T-bar quadrupeds, TenseBot, Spherobot, Mori & Hirose helical tensegrity, EVA series, snake/worm tensegrity robots), tensegrity wings/UAVs, tensegrity grippers, soft-tensegrity manipulators, MEMS / micro-tensegrities, origami- and kirigami-tensegrity hybrids, knitted / woven tensegrity textiles, and lattice/metamaterial tensegrities; (7) Tensegrity space structures and large deployable tensegrities (NASA TIPS, ESA tensegrity boom, Tibert/Pellegrino deployable masts, lunar/Mars habitats, Skelton's tensegrity wheel, ChemRover); (8) Modular and self-assembling tensegrities, including TetraSpine, ReBOT, and recent (2022-2026) work on adaptive, morphing, self-stressed, and energy-harvesting tensegrities; (9) Tensegrity-inspired metamaterials and architected unit cells used in additive manufacturing (3D-printed multi-material PETG/TPU and elastomer-rigid composites), including Fraternali, Rimoli, Pajunen, Pal et al. work on tensegrity lattices for impact absorption and wave control; (10) Non-Snelson topology generation methods (Tensegrity_gen, topology optimization, evolutionary search, machine-learning generative tensegrity design from 2020 onwards).

For each design family, give: design name + standard reference, node/strut/cable counts, characteristic geometric parameters and constraints, prestress / form-finding requirements, known self-equilibrated configurations, and at least one reference image with figure caption / source attribution (cite the original paper or open archive). Where possible include open-source / permissively-licensed sources (NASA NTRTsim, MOTES, Tensegrity_gen, Berkeley ULTRA-Spine, the Snelson archive, GrabCAD / Thingiverse) and indicate which designs have publicly available CAD / STL / URDF / mesh files.

Conclude with concrete recommendations for the BYU Mentored Research Grant project on multi-material 3D-printed tensegrity (PETG struts + TPU tendons, Bambu Lab H2D printer, target application: impact-absorbing crutch tip and architected energy-absorbing lattices): which 5-10 tensegrity designs would be most promising as starting geometries for parametric / Bayesian-optimization design exploration, with rationale and the specific geometric/material parameters that should be exposed as design variables.
